A record El Niño is likely to temporarily push 2027 to temperatures we're only expecting in the late 2030s. It's a rare chance to learn how big El Niño can get.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The supercharged El Niño building in the Pacific is likely to make 2027 the warmest year on record, about 3 degrees Fahrenheit (1.7 degrees Celsius) warmer than the late 1800s. At today's rate of warming, the long-term average will not reach that level until the late 2030s.

We should treat this preview as a test to understand just how big these events can get. That means writing down what we expect now and then learning from what happens, so we can act in time when the next major event hits.

El Niño is a natural swing in the tropical Pacific that's part of the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO). During El Niño, trade winds, which normally blow from east to west along the equator, weaken. Warm water spreads east, and heat stored below the ocean surface escapes into the air. The World Meteorological Organization expects the central equatorial Pacific to average about 6.7 F (3.7 C) above normal from October to December this year, against a previous record of about 4.5 F (2.5 C) for a monthly average and 5.4 F (3.0 C) for a single week, both in late 2015.

This is looking to be an extraordinary event with severe impacts. It's predicted we'll see widespread extreme weather, including wildfires, droughts and floods in Australia, Africa, Asia and South America. Crop production is expected to fall in major breadbaskets like India and Southeast Asia, disrupting food supplies and driving up prices. One forecast even suggested there could be over 450,000 heat-related deaths by February because of the additional warming from El Niño.

We can use this extreme event to further develop and improve the models we use to forecast strong El Niño events, and to better understand the impacts we're likely to see. Three findings from one of my ongoing research projects shape how I think we should use this winter.

First, the long-term temperature record we plan with is out of date. Studies have suggested that the Pacific changed in the late 1970s. According to a simple physical model, before 1980, an El Niño that warms the central Pacific above 5.4 F (3 C) was considered a once-in-1,500-year event. From 1980, it became about once in 60 years. This change lies mainly in the ocean, which since 1980 has held on to its extra warmth for about 1.5 years, rather than the 1.1 years it previously did. Plans built on the full historical record may underestimate the next El Niño , so we should be concentrating on models that represent the recent conditions.

Second, El Niño may have a ceiling, and we still need to understand what sets it. Normally the western Pacific is much warmer than the east. That temperature difference is what keeps the trade winds blowing. El Niño grows by weakening those winds, which lets warm water spread east. But as the east warms, the difference shrinks, so El Niño uses up the very thing it feeds on.

You can see this in the chart below. Over the past 76 years, every 1.8 F (1 C) of El Niño warming has shrunk the difference by about the same amount. At that rate, the difference runs out when the central Pacific is about 7 F (4 C) warmer than normal in the autumn months, when El Niño peaks, and as little as 3 F (2 C) in spring. No El Niño on record has gotten there in the season when events still grow. Two events, in 1983 and 1998, did run out of difference, but only in spring, when El Niño fades anyway, and both faded. This year's event has come closer than any other while still growing: in September it had the least difference left (just 0.6 C or 1.08 F) of any September on record. We will post our prediction before the peak. If El Niño keeps growing after the difference is gone, we are wrong.

The further right a dot is, the stronger the El Niño. The lower it is, the smaller the temperature difference between the warm western and the cooler eastern Pacific. Each grey dot is one month since 1950. As El Niño grows, the dots slide down towards zero, where the difference runs out, at about 6 to 7 F (3.2 to 3.9 C) above normal in autumn and about 3 F (2 C) in spring. No El Niño has gone past that point. This year’s event (red) is the closest yet while still growing.

Third, artificial intelligence (AI) — a tool increasingly used for El Niño forecasts — is not a silver bullet either. In a 2025 study, an AI weather model trained without the strongest hurricanes could not forecast them. We see a similar limit in our El Niño tests. A model that learns only from a record that does not contain a large number of extreme events cannot always say how high El Niño can go. Models that instead build in the physics of an event, such as the east–west difference, are still our best bet for predicting strong El Niño events. The best forecasts this winter are likely to combine the two. So what should we do with this year?

We need to be honest about the limits of our own models. Every forecast of this event — whether a simple physical model, an AI model or a full climate model — is being pushed beyond the range of events it was built and tested on. Where these models disagree, they are telling us where predictability runs out. Ranges of uncertainty are equally important as forecasts, and plans should be made with both in mind.

Crops, rivers, power grids and human bodies respond to the heat they get, whether that heat is caused by an annual fluctuation or a long-term change in climate.

Nations also need to be ready to assess these events, both before and after they occur. In June, the U.K.'s Government Office for Science brought scientists, forecasters and industry experts together. Its findings trace the risks to the U.K. through food, farming and energy, and warn that a very large El Niño "could result in unforeseen effects" on U.K. weather. Assessments like this should be standard for every government. Before the peak, forecasters, health services, utilities and food agencies should publish what they expect, and afterwards assess how the reality compared to the predictions.

Finally, we should improve our models by measuring the event as closely as we can. The buoys, floats and satellites watching the Pacific are recording what may be the largest El Niño of the modern era, and that record will train and test the next generation of models.

None of this works if each group acts alone. National weather services turn forecasts into warnings. People in government, industry and local services know what a failed harvest or a gas shortage costs. Scientists can test where prediction stops working, which is exactly where an event this size sits. These groups should agree before the peak what they will measure and how they will judge the forecasts, and meet again once it has passed.

Critics will make two points. The first is that one El Niño year is not a 2030s climate. Its heat, droughts and floods fall in particular places, while long-term warming spreads differently, so the preview does not apply to every region. The second is that the numbers are uncertain. A simple model like ours, an AI model and a full climate model can each give a different ceiling.

Both points are fair, but neither argument weakens the case. Crops, rivers, power grids and human bodies respond to the heat they get, whether that heat is caused by an annual fluctuation or a long-term change in climate. A 3 F annual rise due to El Niño affects those systems in the same way as a 3 F rise due to climate change will, only with less time to adapt. The El Niños of 1982 to 1983 and 1997 to 1998 cost the world economy an estimated $9.8 trillion in lost income between them, according to one study. As for uncertainty, the answer is to run as many simulations with as many different tools as we can, and to treat their spread as the measure of what we do not know. When models disagree, the real event is an excellent test bed to find out which one was most accurate.

This winter, the Pacific will run an experiment we could never run ourselves. Either result will teach us something. If El Niño stops growing where the physics says it should, we gain a way to put an upper limit on the worst case. If it breaks through, the worst case is worse than our records show, and every plan built on those records needs revisiting. By this time next year we will know which model of El Niño came closest — and how well we coped with a year from the 2030s.

#6335. Astronomer Isabel Angelo hunts for odd signals in telescope data

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

A comet or a newborn star might explain an odd signal in telescope data. Astrophysicist Isabel Angelo is looking for signals that defy those familiar explanations.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Isabel Angelo spends her days searching the cosmos for exoplanets and signs of extraterrestrial intelligence. But Angelo’s head isn’t in the stars. It’s buried under mountains of 0s and 1s — data from space telescopes old and new.

To piece together a fuller picture of what’s out there (alien megastructures around nearby stars, perhaps?), Angelo and her colleagues at the SETI Institute in Mountain View, Calif., are turning to machine learning models. These tools are analyzing the troves of telescope data for anomalies — things that look “weird” in space that we don’t know how to explain yet.

Most of the space weirdos will probably turn out to be total normies — a comet, a newborn star or a star surrounded by lots of gas and dust. “These are things that I would expect [the models] to find,” Angelo says. “But the goal is to find something that’s not even in any of these categories.”

In the meantime, Angelo keeps her whimsy and wonder for space alive by remembering historic moments, like the reveal of the first portrait of a black hole in 2019. The scientists “put all of these telescopes all over the Earth. They wait for the Earth to rotate. They do all this math to construct this one image,” Angelo says. “I can’t believe how creative and innovative we have to be to learn about space. It’s such a specific and really fun challenge.”

A woman's heart issues seemed to be tied to her rapid gulping of ice-cold drinks.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The patient: A 46-year-old woman in California

The symptoms: After an uneventful 10-hour work shift, the woman was walking to her car and drinking an ice-cold beverage when a sudden, burning pain struck the middle of her chest. The pain spread to both of her forearms and lasted about 20 minutes.

About 10 minutes after this pain began, she started sweating and felt nauseated and lightheaded, as though she might pass out.

What happened next: The pain continued as the woman began driving home, so she changed course and instead drove to the nearest emergency department.

An electrocardiogram (EKG), which records the heart's electrical activity, showed subtle abnormalities. A blood test for troponin, a protein released into the bloodstream when heart muscle is damaged, was normal. However, a second troponin test taken before she left the hospital came back elevated after she had been discharged. Doctors called her about the new results and advised her to drive to the nearest emergency department.

There, a third blood test showed that her troponin level had risen even further, and doctors diagnosed a heart attack. An angiogram — a scan that shows the structure of blood vessels — revealed a small tear in a branch of her right coronary artery, which supplies blood to the heart.

About 30 hours after she was discharged, the woman developed similar chest pain after taking several gulps of ice-cold green tea and subsequently jogging up a flight of stairs. The pain began when she reached the top of the stairs and was accompanied by the same lightheaded feeling she had experienced before.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

She called 911 and was again brought to an emergency department, and although an initial EKG showed no clear signs of a heart attack, subsequent recordings revealed heart-activity changes consistent with one. A second angiogram revealed a new tear in the left circumflex artery, a branch of the left coronary artery.

The woman developed tears in both her right and left coronary arteries, which supply the heart with oxygen-rich blood.

The diagnosis: Doctors diagnosed the woman with spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD), a condition in which a tear develops in the wall of a coronary artery. In SCAD, blood collects within the artery wall, and this compresses the channel that blood normally flows through to reach the heart. As in the patient's case, this compression can sometimes trigger heart attacks by drastically restricting the heart's blood supply.

Doctors also found fibromuscular dysplasia (FMD) in a blood vessel in the woman's pelvis. FMD changes the structure of artery walls, making them too weak or too stiff, and it's known to occur in some people with SCAD. It may have made her arteries more prone to tearing, the doctors wrote in a report of the case.

The treatment: During her first emergency department visit, doctors gave the woman aspirin, fluids, medicine for nausea and an antacid. Her chest pain eventually went away. At the second visit, doctors gave her the blood thinner heparin to reduce blood clotting and the beta-blocker metoprolol to slow her heart rate. She was discharged the following morning with prescriptions for cholesterol- and blood-pressure-lowering drugs.

After the second episode, doctors gave her opioid painkillers and medicine for nausea to take as needed, along with aspirin and a cholesterol-lowering drug. The cholesterol-lowering drug was soon stopped because she did not have high cholesterol. Doctors eventually stopped the blood-pressure medication, too, after a follow-up heart ultrasound showed that the affected part of her heart was moving normally again.

She continued taking nebivolol, a different beta-blocker that slows the heart rate and can reduce stress on the organ, for years after these two episodes. And for several months after the second episode, the woman avoided cold drinks on her own initiative. She gradually reintroduced them, taking small sips rather than gulping. Ten years later, she remained free of symptoms, the report noted.

What makes this case unique: Years later, the woman learned that cold drinks had been linked to atrial fibrillation (AFib), an irregular heart rhythm. She told her healthcare team that she suspected cold drinks might have triggered SCAD in her case, too.

Separately, a 2017 case report described another woman who developed chest pain and a heart attack after drinking cold water. Doctors subsequently found that she had SCAD and FMD. However, that report did not investigate cold water as a possible trigger of the patient's symptoms.

The authors of the current report proposed that rapidly swallowing a cold drink may trigger a brief rise in blood pressure, known as a pressor response. This is associated with increased activation of the body's fight-or-flight system, which can then release stress hormones. These changes may make the heart contract more forcefully and cause the coronary arteries to narrow temporarily, thereby increasing the forces acting on their walls. In someone whose arteries are susceptible to tears, that added stress could contribute to rips in the tissue and the accumulation of blood within the artery wall.

However, the report authors stressed that they cannot establish that cold drinks caused the woman's dissections in this instance. They hope their findings will encourage doctors to ask patients with SCAD about potential triggers, but they said further research is needed to determine whether rapidly drinking cold beverages can really trigger the condition.

#6330. Motion under the ocean explains the depth of the world’s deepest spot

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

A tight bend in the subducting Pacific plate may help explain Challenger Deep

The ROV Jason/Medea (Jason shown here during a 2021 dive at the East Pacific Rise) can descend up to 6,500 meters below the ocean surface. In a new study, it helped researchers discover volcanic deposits in the Mariana Trench.

D. Fornari, WHOI-SSSG, MISO Facility, NDSF Jason Team, NSF

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Challenger Deep is the deepest valley in the deepest trench in the ocean, plunging to roughly 11,000 meters below sea level.

Now, scientists have a new clue about how it got to be so … well, deep.

Challenger Deep is found within the Mariana Trench, a crescent-shaped gouge in the seafloor east of the Philippines in the Pacific Ocean. The trench is the scene of a slo-mo tectonic collision called a subduction zone: The Pacific plate is diving beneath the Mariana plate, bending downward as it sinks into the mantle, forming a steep trench on the ocean floor.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

All subduction zones are deep, but “it’s interesting why this is the deepest spot in the Earth’s ocean,” says geoscientist Robert Stern, an emeritus professor at the University of Texas at Dallas and a visiting researcher at the University of California, Los Angeles.

He and colleagues employed a remotely operated robot called ROV Jason/Medea to descend to more than 6,000 meters and explore the Mariana Trench seafloor around the edges of Challenger Deep. The rocks turned out to contain pyroclastic deposits, evidence of an erstwhile explosive volcanic eruption. Those deposits included platelike blocks that could indicate eruption pulses, and lobe-shaped rocks where the volcanic flows ended and quickly cooled.

These are the deepest pyroclastic deposits found on Earth, the scientists report November 23 in Frontiers in Earth Science.

How explosive an eruption is at Earth’s surface depends on the chemical makeup of the magma. When the molten rock contains a high proportion of volatile gases, including water vapor, those gases suddenly expand when the magma reaches the surface, producing a violent explosion.

Such explosive volcanism shouldn’t be possible in the deep sea; the pressure is too high for any escaping gases to expand, Stern says. Along with that mystery, the volcanic deposits were found unusually close to the trench, compared with what would be expected for a subduction zone.

Stern and his colleagues developed a hypothesis that incorporates these disparate pieces of evidence: The extreme depth of Challenger Deep, they say, may be at least partially due to an especially sharp bend in the Pacific Plate as it sinks into the mantle.

That tighter bend would explain why volcanism is happening closer to the subduction zone than usual. The classic subduction zone scenario is that the sinking plate heats up and melts partially as it descends; the magma rises through the overhanging plate and erupts, forming volcanic island arcs several hundred kilometers from the collision zone. Here, the volcanic deposits were just a hundred kilometers or so from the trench — which makes sense if the plate is dipping more steeply.

As for the pyroclastics, “we can’t answer if the eruptions were really explosive,” Stern says. But at those pressures, any gases such as water vapor contained in the magma wouldn’t be able to explosively expand as they would at the surface.

Instead, the pyroclastic rocks might have formed through a new version of deep-sea eruption, one in which water emerging from the magma is initially in a supercritical fluid state. That would minimize any explosive expansion during the eruption and could also produce fragmented, dense deposits like those seen by Jason/Medea.

The discovery of deep-sea pyroclastics is “surprising and unprecedented,” says William Chadwick, a geologist at Oregon State University in Newport. Challenger Deep may be the only place on Earth “with the ingredients to produce explosive volcanism in the super-deep ocean,” he says. “Imagining this happening is … pretty mind-boggling.”

A lot more work remains to be done to evaluate all of these new ideas, Stern says. “But a lot of things are now coming together.”

#6329. The Sky Today on Thursday, November 26: Thanksgiving turkey in the sky

Looking for a sky event this week? Check out our full Sky This Week column.

Celebrate Thanksgiving with a celestial turkey: The famous Orion Nebula (M42) is also playfully known as the Turkey Nebula because it looks to some like a turkey, particularly in deep astrophotos. But whether you’re a photographer or not, this bright deep-sky treat is easy to enjoy tonight while dinner digests.

By about 9 P.M. local time, Orion the Hunter has risen above the eastern horizon, his recognizable three-star belt standing in a vertical line. The lowest star in that line is Alnitak (Zeta [ζ] Orionis), and the Orion Nebula lies just 3.7° south-southwest of this star, to its lower right on the sky this evening. You might be able to spot its glow without optical aid, although the bright Moon nearby may make that difficult. Binoculars or any telescope will easily show it.

At 4th magnitude and spanning some 85’ by 60’, the Orion Nebula is a huge and bright star-forming region that sits roughly 1,350 light-years from Earth. In the brightest portion of the nebula lies a small grouping of young stars called the Trapezium Cluster. Take your time with this gorgeous sight, scanning around the region to pick out detail in the nebulosity. And if you are an astrophotographer, consider turning the view into a Thanksgiving memory to share for years to come.

One tooth from a cave in southern China may upend how we think about early human origins in Asia.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In a cave in southern China, archaeologists have discovered an unusual 100,000-year-old tooth that may add a brand-new branch to the human family tree. A genetic analysis of the enamel revealed that the tooth is distinct from all other examples discovered in the area and may have come from an individual who belonged to a previously unknown ancient human lineage.

In a study published Wednesday (Nov. 25) in the journal Nature, researchers described four isolated teeth recovered from two cave sites in southern China that date to around 100,000 years ago, when our extinct cousins the Denisovans roamed Asia. Teeth from one cave site are similar to Denisovans', but a tooth from the second site has a unique shape and genetic variants in the tooth enamel, suggesting it is from an "unresolved archaic Homo" group, the researchers wrote.

The teeth were recovered from archaeological cave sites named Longchuandong and Chuanshandong in the Guangxi region. Based on uranium-series dating, the two teeth from Longchuandong — a molar and a bicuspid (the teeth between the canines and molars) — date to about 104,500 to 42,600 years ago, while the two teeth from Chuanshandong — which are both bicuspids — are at least 100,800 years old.

To try to figure out which ancient human group these teeth belonged to, the researchers studied the shape and characteristics of the teeth and extracted proteins from the tooth enamel. The heritable traits of the two Longchuandong teeth lined up well with Denisovan teeth that had previously been identified, revealing that a Denisovan-related group was living in southern China in the Late Pleistocene (129,000 to 11,700 years ago), according to the study. But the Chuanshandong teeth — which the team thinks may be from the same individual — were very different.

The shape of the Chuanshandong bicuspids "did not align well with any established East Asian Homo member," the researchers wrote. For example, the Chuanshandong teeth had a complex tooth root system typically seen in Homo erectus, but they also had traits more aligned with Homo sapiens, including a more symmetrically shaped tooth crown.

The root system of the Chuanshandong tooth was complex and similar to what experts see in Homo erectus.

The researchers extracted proteins from the Longchuandong teeth and one of the Chuanshandong bicuspids and discovered they were all from chromosomally male individuals. But while the Longchuandong proteins matched those from Denisovan remains that were unearthed elsewhere in China, several of the Chuanshandong protein variants have only been identified in H. erectus and Homo antecessor, an ancient human distantly related to Neanderthals and modern humans.

The protein analysis "showed that Chuanshandong formed a sister group to the common ancestors of Neanderthals, Denisovans and H. sapiens," the researchers wrote in the study. This means that "at least two non-sapiens Homo populations may have existed in southern China's subtropics during the Middle and Late Pleistocene," they wrote.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Given the small number of 100,000-year-old fossils from China that have been analyzed to date, it is unclear what the morphology and genetics of the Chuanshandong teeth mean for our understanding of human evolution, researchers say.

Denisovans were first identified in 2010, when DNA analysis of a tiny pinkie finger bone found in a Siberian cave revealed that the group was distinct from Neanderthals and modern humans. Since then, paleoanthropologists have discovered fossils all across Asia from our extinct cousins and learned that Denisovans, Neanderthals and modern humans all interbred when they had the chance. But Denisovans' and Neanderthals' genetics are known from full genomes — the complete set of their genetic material — while due to preservation issues, most of the fossils from China have only produced proteomes, a more limited set of genetic data that provides information on the body's proteins.

The Chuanshandong proteome included an ancestral genetic variant linking them to H. erectus and H. antecessor, two groups that lived before H. sapiens arrived on the scene. The presence of these variants suggests that the Chuanshandong teeth were from someone who belonged to a primitive Homo lineage, the researchers wrote. Their unique ancient proteins could also be explained by interbreeding with H. erectus.

It's not clear whether they are our cousins.

It's too early, though, to call this a new human group, study co-author Qiaomei Fu, director of the Ancient DNA Laboratory at the Institute of Vertebrate Paleontology and Paleoanthropology, part of the Chinese Academy of Sciences, told Live Science in an email.

"We could call it the Chuanshandong group temporarily, but we need more fossil and molecular evidence to determine its affinity with other archaic Homo," Fu said. "It's not clear whether they are our cousins."

The Guangxi region of China is known for its caves, many of which have Pleistocene mammal fossils.

The new Chuanshandong proteome is extremely interesting, said John Hawks, an anthropologist at the University of Wisconsin-Madison who was not involved in the study. But "the paper characterizes this as an 'unknown Homo'. I wouldn't put it that way. The question is which group has variation of the proteome," he told Live Science in an email.

Hawks noted that it is currently unclear whether H. erectus or Denisovans had the specific variant identified in the Chuanshandong tooth, as paleoproteomic analysis is still a relatively new technique. If the genetic variant existed in H. erectus, then the Chuanshandong teeth, which are more similar to H. erectus in shape than they are to Neanderthals, may actually be from an H. erectus individual rather than a brand-new human group. But the comparison is further complicated by the fact that no one has yet found other Denisovan bicuspids — the type of tooth found in the Chuanshandong cave.

"I have a feeling that a comprehensive analysis with all the teeth together would be stronger than these separate papers" that Fu's research team has published recently, Hawks said. "I think there is more to learn from compiling more complete analyses."

The researchers noted in the study that excavations have been ongoing in Guangxi caves for a decade, revealing a rich variety of Pleistocene mammal fossils, including ancient human relatives. This may mean that the pace of discoveries about our species' past will soon accelerate.

"We have some new findings from this region, and we are conducting analyses on them," Fu said.

#6327. Nov. 26, 2018: Mars InSight lander touches down

InSight, short for Interior Exploration using Seismic Investigations, Geodesy, and Heat Transport, landed on Mars Nov. 26, 2018, tasked with a simple yet challenging mission: unlock the mysteries of Mars’ interior. Top priorities included uncovering Mars’ internal structure by measuring the thickness of the crust, obtaining the size and density of the core, and sussing out the structure and composition of Mars’ mantle.

In addition to bountiful seismic data, which included more than 1,300 marsquakes, InSight recorded about a year’s worth of weather data at the lander’s location with unprecedented accuracy, according to Bruce Banerdt, the mission’s principal investigator and principal research scientist. The InSight lander also took the first magnetic field measurements on the surface of Mars and measured several properties of the soil around it.

Not everything was a rousing success, however. Most famously, the mission’s “mole” subsurface probe only penetrated about 16 inches (40 centimeters) deep, despite being designed to burrow to a depth of at least 3 feet (10 meters). It turned out that the soil beneath InSight’s struts was unlike any previously encountered on the surface; it simply didn’t cooperate with the instrument’s design. But even that cloud has a silver lining, as it provided scientists with important details about the terrain upon which InSight landed.

InSight’s successful initial two-year mission was extended to run at least through the end of December 2022. But the stationary lander relied on power generated from its two large solar panels, which steadily gathered dust. That dust reduced the panels’ efficiency over time, forcing mission planners to make tough choices regarding power allotment. In May of 2022, engineers placed the craft’s robotic arm into a final resting pose and turned off all its instruments, save one: InSight’s seismometer continued to operate on what little power was available, running about half the time, according to Banerdt. InSight last contacted Earth Dec. 15, 2022, after which two attempts were made to raise the lander. Both failed, and a few days later, NASA officially brought the mission to a close.

Alison Klesman is senior editor of Astronomy magazine. She holds a Ph.D. in astronomy and has studied a variety of topics, from minor planets to supermassive black holes.

#6325. ‘Mitt & Ted’ recounts how a political odd couple changed U.S. health care

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The Big Dig podcast host Ian Coss explores how Mitt Romney and Ted Kennedy worked together to reform American health care laws

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

In 1973, U.S. Senator Ted Kennedy often visited the cancer ward at Boston Children’s Hospital, where his eldest son was battling osteosarcoma. Kennedy witnessed other parents on the ward make impossible decisions regarding their child’s care when insurance didn’t cover it. Their stories lit a fire within the senator that burned bright for the rest of his life.

Kennedy spent decades fighting for health care reform, representing his home state of Massachusetts. He even teamed up with a former political rival from across the aisle: Mitt Romney. The story of this unexpected alliance is recounted in Mitt & Ted, the newest season of the GBH News podcast The Big Dig. Over eight episodes, journalist and host Ian Coss explores how their work laid the foundation for the Affordable Care Act, one of the most significant and divisive health care reforms in U.S. history.

We first meet Romney as a young upstart Republican challenger vying to flip Kennedy’s Senate seat in 1994. The race seemed close until a legendary debate. Romney had Kennedy on the defensive until the sitting senator pivoted to the issue near and dear to his heart: health care.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

“Kennedy is the elder statesman, in command of the issue,” Coss says. “Romney is like an eager student trying to pass the test.” Using his deep knowledge, Kennedy buries the less experienced Romney. In the election, Kennedy then beat Romney by a landslide, even when many Democrats were ousted by Republican challengers that same year. But the loss may have motivated Romney to keep going.

Several years later, Romney unexpectedly became a champion of health care reform as the newly elected governor of Massachusetts. The state’s health care system was facing the potential loss of about a billion dollars in federal funding, threatening hospitals that served vulnerable populations. Romney’s administration created Romneycare, which was supported by three features: individual and employer mandates, affordable options for low-income people, and a health care exchange where people could compare plans from different providers.

With Senator Kennedy’s help, the groundbreaking law passed in 2006 and expanded health insurance coverage to 98 percent of Massachusetts’ population.

Romneycare gained national attention and kicked off years-long efforts to replicate it on the federal level. Finally, in 2010, President Obama signed the Affordable Care Act, or ACA. Modeled on Romneycare, the law (colloquially called Obamacare) adapted the reforms made in Massachusetts for all 50 states, a challenge since many states had larger shares of uninsured people than Massachusetts had even before Romneycare.

The Democrats in Congress also sought to include a government insurance plan in the reform, similar to Medicaid but available to more people. Republicans were wary of the ACA generally, but a government-provided insurance option was a line they wouldn’t cross. The ACA eventually passed without the public option, but by then the political winds had shifted. If there ever was a chance to secure bipartisan support for the law, it was gone by the time Democrats were willing to compromise on the public option. And as soon as the ACA became law, Republicans started fighting it.

The podcast traces an impressive number of political twists and turns on this health care reform journey. Though I got turned around a few times, I never fully lost the plot thanks to Coss’ well-placed reminders and takeaways.

Beyond the story of Romney and Kennedy, the podcast gives voice to many more people who made the ACA a reality: government workers who went from foes to allies who enlisted unlikely help from the conservative Heritage Foundation; longtime friends in the Massachusetts state legislature who were driven apart by the reform; a father who struggled to afford health care and how he advocated for reform with his church. I teared up more than once listening to the human stories behind these policy changes.

Overall, Mitt & Ted gave me new appreciation for why passing a reform is so difficult, despite how life-changing and life-saving access to health care can be. The series points to moments when stars aligned to make reform possible and suggests that more of those opportunities lie ahead.

“The work of American health care remains very much unfinished,” Coss says. “When the perfect alignment of frustration and opportunity arrives again, that might be what determines whether our leaders actually work together.”

#6324. The closest exoplanets may host magnetic fields

In all the universe, Earth is the only planet known to have life. A big part of the reason life is possible here is our planet’s magnetic field. It acts like a shield, deflecting harmful energy from our Sun as well as cosmic rays from deep space that could otherwise erode Earth’s atmosphere and irradiate the surface, a death sentence for evolving life-forms.

But Earth is far from the only planet we know of. As of this writing, there are more than 6,300 confirmed exoplanets on the roster, with more added by the day. Scientists have discovered stars with as many planets as our own Sun hosts. In other systems, planets as big as Jupiter whip around their sun in only a few days’ time. Astronomers have even discovered planets that orbit multiple stars at once, and they recently caught a glimpse of a possible atmosphere around a rocky, Earth-sized world in its star’s habitable zone. But until 2026, they had no compelling evidence that any terrestrial exoplanets had magnetic fields of their own.

Because of their protective role, magnetic fields have major implications in the search for life beyond Earth. Astronomers have long suspected that part of the reason Mars now appears dead is that its magnetic field fizzled out billions of years ago. This let the solar wind strip the water and other volatile compounds from its atmosphere, leaving it cold and barren.

Beyond the solar system, in 2019 researchers reported “indirect detections of exoplanetary magnetic fields” in four hot Jupiters. Then, a 2021 study found a strong signature of a magnetic field around HAT-P-11 b, a Neptune-like planet. Two years later, a pair of studies detected possible signs of a magnetic field around YZ Ceti b — this time, a rocky, Earth-like planet roughly the same size as, and only a bit less massive than our own. But this find has not yet been confirmed.

In July 2026, a study published in Astronomy & Astrophysics found possible evidence of magnetic fields around two rocky exoplanets. Not just any exoplanets, either — Proxima Centauri b and d, the closest confirmed planets beyond our solar system, orbiting the red dwarf Proxima Centauri 4.2 light-years away.

Proxima b, roughly Earth’s mass and size, orbits every 11.1 days. Proxima d, likely a quarter to a third of our planet’s mass and 70% its size, orbits closer in with a period of 5.1 days. Because Proxima Centauri is smaller and less massive than our Sun, Proxima b is inside the habitable zone, where temperatures allow liquid surface water. A third planet, Proxima c, was tentatively detected in 2019 but is still unconfirmed. Astronomers don’t yet know if any of these worlds host atmospheres.

The new study, led by María Rosa Zapatero Osorio of the Centro de Astrobiología in Madrid, Spain, used 117 separate observations made with the Echelle SPectrograph for Rocky Exoplanets and Stable Spectroscopic Observations (ESPRESSO) instrument on the Very Large Telescope atop Cerro Paranal in Chile. The research followed up on previous studies conducted with ESPRESSO in 2020 and 2022, which focused on confirming the presence of planets around Proxima Centauri. Zapatero Osorio and her collaborators used the data to identify a peculiar correlation between the timing of flares emitted from Proxima Centauri and the orbital periods of its planets.

“We detected low-energy flares occurring with a characteristic period of about 5.1 days,” Zapatero Osorio says. “This is very close to Proxima d’s orbital period.” But flares did not occur during every orbit of Proxima d, so the team ran statistical analyses to determine whether the flares were preferentially occurring at particular phases of the planet’s orbit. They found strong statistical evidence “that the occurrence of the flares is not randomly distributed over the planet’s orbital period,” Zapatero Osorio says. “Instead, a significant number of flares tend to occur at particular times in Proxima d’s orbit.” This is a possible indication that Proxima d could be interacting magnetically with its parent star, which would be likely to happen if the planet has a strong magnetic field of its own.

Using a model adapted from the physics of solar flares, Zapatero Osorio’s team calculated that Proxima d could have a magnetic field anywhere from 8 to 230 gauss in strength, with the best median estimate limited to around 16 gauss. This is about 27 times more powerful than Earth’s magnetic field (0.6 gauss), which protects life on Earth from the worst of the Sun’s energy.

Their model assumes that the star and planet are magnetically connected, Zapatero Osorio says. Each sustains its own magnetic field, and these fields are interconnected. As a result of this connection, stress builds up on the stellar surface. From time to time, this stress is released in the form of low-energy flares, whose period is closely tied to the planet’s orbital period.

Although there was not as strong a correlation between Proxima b’s orbital period and the stellar flares, the team did find that Proxima b could also be interacting with the star, albeit in a lesser capacity. This suggests that although the finding is less sure, Proxima b may also sustain a magnetic field.

There are alternative explanations for the findings. One possibility is that there could be intrinsic, long-lived active regions on Proxima Centauri itself that account for the peculiar timing of the flares. Another explanation is that gravitational interactions between the planets and Proxima Centauri could induce disturbances on the star without requiring a strong planetary magnetosphere, although the team suggests this is less likely. It’s also possible that when Proxima’s stellar wind reaches the planets, it interacts with them in a way that mimics the effects of a planetary magnetic field without requiring one.

Like most red dwarfs, Proxima is a highly active star, regularly belching out intense flares that would be hazardous to any fledgling life-forms on the worlds in close orbit. Because Proxima is so close to Earth and has at least one rocky planet in its habitable zone, it makes a perfect testbed for studying how stellar flares could affect habitability around red dwarfs — the most common stars in the universe.

Astronomers looking for habitable worlds around these stars must contend with the likelihood that any planets would be effectively sterilized by the intense radiation in the flares constantly washing over them. Now, though, there is a glimmer of hope. If Proxima b and d do have magnetic fields, as this research suggests, they could act much like Earth’s own protective magnetic shield, deflecting enough harmful stellar radiation that life might just be able to take hold.

“Earth’s magnetic field plays an important role in protecting life and supporting human progress,” says Zapatero Osorio. “It shields our planet from the solar wind and energetic particles, and it has also played an important role in navigation.”

Unfortunately, Proxima d is so close to its host star that it is likely too hot to sustain life as we know it. Proxima b, however, lies within the habitable zone. “Based on the results of our study, both Proxima d and b may have magnetospheres capable of providing some protection against their host star’s activity,” Zapatero Osorio says.

The importance of this find goes deeper than simply a pair of neighboring planets. In the last few years, evidence has emerged that gas giant exoplanets similar to Jupiter and Saturn host magnetic fields. These are the easiest types of planets to detect and study, but while magnetic fields around such worlds are certainly fascinating, the implications for planetary habitability are limited.

But as the number of known planets continues to swell, so, too, does our sample of Earth-like worlds. And if the two closest rocky planets beyond our solar system do indeed have magnetic fields, then perhaps these features are common. If true, it increases the chances that rocky worlds across the galaxy could be habitable — at least, for life-forms as we understand them. And the more planets capable of hosting life, the more likely it is that we might someday discover we are not alone.

Nick Oakes is a science writer for NASA’s Heliophysics Education Activation Team at Goddard Space Flight Center in Greenbelt, Maryland.

Exceptionally high tides, El Niño-fueled conditions and abnormally warm water are converging on California's coast, with authorities urging residents to limit unnecessary travel this Thanksgiving.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Major flooding of up to 2.7 feet (0.8 meters) is expected in parts of California today (Nov. 25) as record-breaking tides, El Niño-fueled conditions and warmer-than-average ocean water converge along the state's coast.

The triple flooding threat is expected to hit the San Francisco Bay Area especially hard, with San Francisco International Airport and other low-lying areas of the city bracing for deluges, while officials warned of dangerous breaking waves measuring 20 to 30 feet (6 to 9 m) tall along San Francisco's coast, the San Francisco Chronicle reported.

Meanwhile, in Southern California, coastal communities should expect potentially record-breaking "king tides" and breaking waves up to 15 feet (4.6 m) high, the National Weather Service warned on its website. King tides are exceptionally high tides that occur every year due to seasonal factors and the alignment of Earth, the sun and the moon — but this year's "super" El Niño has amplified the risk by pushing a massive "Kelvin wave" up California's coast.

Citing the forecast, several cities on California's central coast have closed beaches to shield people from hazards, including sudden waves that could wash beachgoers out to sea. Local authorities have also urged residents to limit unnecessary travel during the Thanksgiving holiday.

"As Californians head into the holiday, take a few minutes to check travel conditions, sign up for local emergency alerts, and make a plan to keep your family safe," California governor Gavin Newsom said in a statement Tuesday (Nov. 24).

The flooding comes as a perfect storm of adverse conditions has gathered on California's coastline. Scientists expected the king tides and the coastal flooding associated with them to emerge this time of the year. However, these powerful tides are now arriving on top of blistering sea temperatures due to accelerating climate change and the current El Niño event — the warm phase of a multiyear natural climate pattern that's in full swing and set to intensify through the end of the year.

Ocean water expands as it warms, swelling tides and raising the risk of strong surf and big waves. As a result, this year's tides are predicted to be at their highest levels since January 1983, when tides also coincided with El Niño-fueled storms, AFP reported.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Record-breaking “king tides,” combined with elevated surf and a large Pacific swell, are expected to bring significant coastal flooding to California during Thanksgiving week.

In January 1983, "all hell broke loose," Reinhard Flick, a researcher at the Scripps Institution of Oceanography at the University of California, San Diego, told AFP. "We had 13-foot (4-meter) waves offshore, the highest tides of the year, and hundreds of millions of dollars in damage. It hit Northern California, Southern California, everybody."

Forecasts suggest this week's conditions won't be quite that bad. But there are risks to be aware of going into winter, especially as El Niño has yet to peak and more king tides are expected in December and January.

"It could potentially be quite bad if we also have rainfall and high waves at the same time during any one of these big events, especially December and January, when rainfall generally increases on our coast," Flick said.

#6322. The Sky This Week from November 27 to December 4: Brilliant Venus

Friday, November 27As fall deepens and winter approaches, the wintertime star patterns are reappearing in our evening sky. One is a large asterism called the Winter Hexagon, now fully above the horizon by about 10 P.M. local time. You should be able to spot this shape even with the Moon nearby, as each point in the Winter Hexagon is a bright, well-known star.

Look east late tonight to locate the waning gibbous Moon near the border of Gemini and Cancer. This will help you find the first point in the Hexagon, the pair of stars Castor and Pollux, the heads of Gemini the Twins, glowing just above the Moon at this time. From there, look upward for another bright star in neighboring Auriga — this is Capella, the next point in the Hexagon. From Capella, look left and down just a little to find the V-shaped face of Taurus the Bull, where the bright star Aldebaran shines, marking the next point. Then it’s down to Orion’s bright knee, Rigel, before you drop down and a little left, close to the horizon, to land on Sirius, the brightest star in the sky and the nose of Canis Major. The Hexagon closes out with the luminary of the Little Dog, Procyon.

Sunrise: 6:59 A.M. Sunset: 4:36 P.M. Moonrise: 7:53 P.M. Moonset: 10:26 A.M. Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (82%) *Times for sunrise, sunset, moonrise, and moonset are given in local time from 40° N 90° W. The Moon’s illumination is given at 10 P.M. local time from the same location.

Saturday, November 28Saturn remains a bright naked-eye object all evening, setting around 2 A.M. local time. Around 8 P.M., you’ll find it high in the south, to the left of the Circlet of Pisces and above the body of Cetus the Whale.

Tonight and for the next few nights, Saturn’s strange, two-faced moon Iapetus is skimming north of the planet, making it easier to find. Now glowing at 11th magnitude, it is heading west toward a late December western elongation, when it will shine about a magnitude brighter but sit far from Saturn. Once you’ve got Saturn in your scope, look about 2’ northeast to land on Iapetus. Over the next few nights, it will move westward, reaching inferior conjunction and standing due north of the ringed world by the 30th.

If you can catch 11th-magnitude Iapetus, you’ll also see four brighter moons: 10th-magnitude Dione, Rhea, and Tethys closer to Saturn; and mid-8th-magnitude Titan, about 3’ to Saturn’s west. The latter is the planet’s largest and brightest moon, easy to spot in any size scope and often even binoculars. If you keep returning each night to track Iapetus, also keep an eye on Titan, which is moving eastward toward the planet and will pass south of Saturn on December 2. Dione, Rhea, and Tethys have smaller orbits and shorter periods, so they move visibly over the course of several hours, frequently swapping places and passing in front of or behind Saturn. For example, Dione disappears behind Saturn’s southwestern limb in an occultation around 12:20 A.M. EST on the 29th (still late on the 28th in time zones farther west).

Sunrise: 7:00 A.M. Sunset: 4:36 P.M. Moonrise: 9:10 P.M. Moonset: 11:09 A.M. Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (73%)

Sunday, November 29Have you ever seen your shadow by planetlight? Venus reaches greatest brilliancy at 2 P.M. EST, now shining at magnitude –4.9. Rising nearly three and a half hours before the Sun, Venus will be so bright that it could potentially cast a shadow if you’re in a location with particularly dark skies (Bortle 1 or 2).

Even without perfect viewing conditions, this morning star can’t be missed. By an hour before sunrise, Venus is roughly 25° high in the southeast, blazing just to the lower left of Spica, the brightest star in Virgo. Far to Venus’ lower left, closer to the ground, Mercury stands nearly 5° above the horizon, shining at magnitude –0.7.

Compare the two planets through a telescope. Venus is a 27%-lit crescent, but its disk stretches 40” across. Mercury, by comparison, is much smaller, just 6” across, but its phase is 82%. Now through the first week of December is the best time to catch the solar system’s smallest planet, as it remains bright but appears to sink toward the horizon day by day. By the 5th, Mercury will be less than 2° high an hour before sunrise, making viewing challenging both because of potential obstacles on the horizon as well as the more turbulent layer of air near the ground.

Venus, meanwhile, stays at roughly the same altitude an hour before sunrise all month, its phase growing to nearly 50% lit by the end of the year. Earth’s sister planet will remain prominent in the morning sky through the first half of next year.

Sunrise: 7:01 A.M. Sunset: 4:36 P.M. Moonrise: 10:25 P.M. Moonset: 11:43 A.M. Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (62%)

Monday, November 30Venus remains a brilliant and unmissable morning star, but it’s not the only object worth paying attention to before dawn. Leo is hosting a celestial get-together this morning as the Moon joins two planets and the star that sits at the heart of the Lion, just beneath the Sickle asterism.

The waning gibbous Moon is the brightest object here; next brightest is Jupiter, located to the Moon’s upper right and glowing at magnitude –2.2. The gas giant stands nearly side by side with Mars (to Jupiter’s left); the Red Planet is fainter but still a respectable magnitude 0.4. Both planets are slowly growing in brightness and size as they approach opposition early next year. Through a telescope, Jupiter stretches 39” across, offering excellent views of its alternating light and dark cloud bands, and Mars is now 8” wide.

Shining between Mars and the Moon is 1st-magnitude Regulus, often drawn as both the heart of Leo and the base of the Sickle asterism’s handle. The curving backward question mark of stars that forms the Sickle’s blade and the Lion’s head in profile lies above the grouping in the sky before dawn.

Sliding along the ecliptic, the Moon passes 1.2° south of Jupiter at 4 A.M. EST, then 1.1° south of Regulus at 10 A.M. EST and 3° south of Mars at 3 P.M. EST.

Sunrise: 7:02 A.M. Sunset: 4:35 P.M. Moonrise: 11:36 P.M. Moonset: 12:11 P.M. Moon Phase: Waning gibbous (51%)

Tuesday, December 1Last Quarter Moon occurs at 1:09 A.M. EST. A few hours later, asteroid 2 Pallas reaches a stationary point at 7 A.M. EST. Located in Cetus, it is visible all evening, setting around 1 A.M. local time. It stands highest around 8 P.M., when it’s roughly 30° above the southern horizon, about 4.2° southeast of 2nd-magnitude Diphda (Beta [β] Ceti).

Glowing at magnitude 9.0, Pallas is easy to find with a small scope. It sits near a neat triangle of 5th- to 6th-magnitude stars, which lie about 1.5° southwest of the asteroid and act as a great reference point to find it tonight. Pallas is 1° east of the easternmost star. Previously, Pallas was closing on that star, moving westward. But after tonight, it will turn and move slowly eastward again, pulling away from the little triangle night by night.

Drop about 5° south of this region for an added treat: 8th-magnitude globular cluster NGC 288, just over the celestial border in Sculptor. Spanning about 13’, this ancient ball of stars lies nearly 49,000 light-years away. It’s also near another deep-sky target, the 7th-magnitude galaxy NGC 253. Often called the Silver Coin or Sculptor Galaxy, this stunning edge-on spiral lies about 1.7° northwest of NGC 288 and can be viewed together with the cluster in wide-field instruments such as binoculars or finder scopes.

Sunrise: 7:03 A.M. Sunset: 4:35 P.M. Moonrise: — Moonset: 12:35 P.M. Moon Phase: Waning crescent (40%)

Wednesday, December 2It’s now asteroid 4 Vesta’s turn to reach a stationary point at 11 A.M. EST as it, too, swims through the domain of Cetus the Whale. Visible in the evening sky, Vesta sits more than 40° above the southern horizon around 7 P.M. local time. Previously moving retrograde, or westward, it will now begin moving prograde, or eastward, against the background stars.

This month Vesta is located roughly halfway between bright Saturn to its northwest and magnitude 3.6 Theta (θ) Ceti to its southeast. Saturn is impossible to miss, as it’s the brightest object in this region of the sky. To locate 7th-magnitude Vesta, find Saturn early in the evening and slide about 8.1° east-southeast to land on the main-belt world. There aren’t a lot of background stars in the immediate vicinity, so try to match your view to the star chart above to locate the asteroid in your eyepiece. Because it’s moving slowly, you’ll need to come back every night or two to check out the view and note the light that’s shifted position — that’s Vesta.

Sunrise: 7:04 A.M. Sunset: 4:35 P.M. Moonrise: 12:43 A.M. Moonset: 12:58 P.M. Moon Phase: Waning crescent (30%)

Thursday, December 3Look north a few hours after sunset to find the W-shaped star pattern of Cassiopeia on her head, looking more like the letter M as this circumpolar constellation swings above the North Celestial Pole. Just 1.9° northwest of Navi (Gamma [γ] Cassiopeiae), the midpoint of the M (or W), is a lovely open cluster cataloged as NGC 225 and known as the Sailboat Cluster.

Longtime Astronomy contributor Rod Pommier gave the cluster its nickname because he saw an arc of stars within the cluster that looked to him like the sail of a boat catching the wind, connected to a straight line of stars forming the mast and another eight stars outlining the vessel itself. The stars of the cluster are roughly 2,100 light-years distant, and this grouping was discovered by Caroline Herschel in 1783.

For added visual interest, the cluster is set against a complex of dark nebulae made of dust, which block the starlight behind them.

Sunrise: 7:05 A.M. Sunset: 4:35 P.M. Moonrise: 1:49 A.M. Moonset: 1:20 P.M. Moon Phase: Waning crescent (21%)

Friday, December 4The waning Moon puts even faint deep-sky objects within reach on these early December evenings. Tonight, let’s look toward a distant elliptical galaxy nestled in the far southeastern corner of Lacerta the Lizard. Cataloged as NGC 7426, this 13th-magnitude stellar smudge sits close to a lovely pair of contrasting stars, making finding it a rewarding sight for all: While you do need a larger scope to track down the galaxy, the stars are visible even through smaller instruments, offering something for everyone.

Around 7 P.M. tonight, our target is still more than 35° high in the west. The zig-zagging figure of Lacerta sits just above cross-shaped Cygnus as the Summer Triangle sinks toward the western horizon. To Lacerta’s left (southeast) is Pegasus, and we’ll use 3rd-magnitude Matar (Eta [η] Pegasi) as our jumping-off point. From here, slide about 5° north-northeast to find a pair of stars, 6th and 8th magnitude, roughly 1’ apart. The brighter star glows blue-white, while its dimmer neighbor shines orangey-gold. NGC 7426 lies roughly 4’ east-northeast of this pair, appearing as a faint, grayish-white smudge. It measures roughly 2’ by 1.5’, its compact size helping to keep its faint light confined to a relatively small area.

Sunrise: 7:06 A.M. Sunset: 4:34 P.M. Moonrise: 2:54 A.M. Moonset: 1:44 P.M. Moon Phase: Waning crescent (14%)

Alison Klesman is senior editor of Astronomy magazine. She holds a Ph.D. in astronomy and has studied a variety of topics, from minor planets to supermassive black holes.

#6321. Kershaw and Civivi Pocket Knives Are on Sale for Black Friday—These Are the Deals Our Gear Editors Trust

Add to your EDC rotation with these picks from Kershaw, Civivi, and more.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Black Friday is a great time to stock up on hobby supplies or even get a jump on holiday shopping—I’m doing both scoping out pocket knives. Like most EDC enthusiasts, no matter how many pocket knives I acquire, there’s room for more, and they make great stocking stuffers. Right now there are a lot of great deals from two of PopMech’s most tested (and beloved!) brands—Kershaw and Civivi.

Between the extensive testing I’ve done, along with intel from Test Editor Justin Park, I’ve rounded up some of the best deals on pocket knives: There are sleek EDC options from Kershaw and Civivi, as well as standout brands like Gerber and Victorinox. If you don’t think you'll use a pocket knife much, I implore you to try one of these—you don’t have to be in the field to reap the benefits of a reliable pocket knife.

I’m a big fan of narrow knives. They remind me of the sleek stiletto blades popular with mobsters, but with modern functionality. The Gerber Pledge hits those old-school notes with better materials like an oxide-coated blade and textured handle. Its barely-there design fits comfortably in your pocket as well.

The Leek’s blade comes to an extremely fine point, ideal for dressing game and gutting fish—like a paring knife built for the outdoors. The blade features assisted opening, meaning easy one-handed deployment, and the stonewashed blade bolsters durability.

The Incindie’s hollow blade not only looks cool but keeps the knife lightweight and offers some grip when slicing. The G10 handle also helps with grip—a lot of my knives have this fiberglass blend material, and it wears in well.

The No. 09 is as functional as it is elegant. The carbon-steel blade is easy to maintain, and the beechwood handle adds a touch of polish. Its rotating collar lock keeps you safe, and the nail indent allows easy blade deployment.

The Blur has a very fine edge that’s easy to sharpen and maintain. A thumb stud makes deployment easy, and the liner lock keeps it in place. The blade itself has a Cerakote coating for extra corrosion resistance.

I love a small pocket knife because they’re so practical, but adding a cat face makes them even more fun to use. Civivi’s Purr is a sub-2-inch blade made of durable Nitro steel with jimping on the spine. Add a grippy G10 handle, and you have an excellent, unique EDC.

The slim profile of the Guile makes it look like a gentleman’s pen knife: easy to slip into the chest pocket of a shirt or jacket. The 14C28N steel blade has excellent edge retention and corrosion resistance, and jimping on the spine for leverage.

The blade deploys with either the thumb hole or the flipper edge on the front.

You can’t go wrong with the classic Swiss Army knife. It’s a knife plus 20 other tools in a small 4.5-inch package. It’s the ultimate multitasker, and the brand has a limited warranty for some peace of mind.

This is a gift-worthy pocket knife you’ll probably want to keep for yourself. The combo of a wooden handle with a Damascus-steel blade marries craftsmanship with practicality.

The Yonder is on the smaller side, with a closed length of just 3.75 inches—excellent for daily compact carry.

Hollowed handles keep a knife lightweight and give it a unique look. The Noctic's skeletal handle is made of Micarta, which helps with grip and develops a patina over time. It also has a finger choil to keep your digits out of the way when slicing.

Jimping (the groove along the spine of the blade) provides leverage when cutting, and the frame lock keeps the blade secured.

This EDC flipper is an excellent choice in an all-black colorway. Its textured handle bolsters grip, and its stonewashed finish adds durability. The blade steel offers excellent corrosion resistance and a hardness level that won’t crack or break.

#6320. The notion of ‘positive masculinity’ is dividing the male studies field

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Researchers’ debate shapes how mental health experts advise men

Does “positive masculinity” exist or reinforce sexist gender norms? Researchers grappling with that question say the answer will help determine how doctors and therapists treat men.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Ryon McDermott set out seven years ago to create a new scale measuring masculinity. McDermott, along with other researchers studying male psyches, was tired of the field’s long-standing assertion that the manlier the man, the worse his outcomes. It was high time to measure masculinity in a positive light.

For almost half a century, the many social science scales that measure gender or masculinity have consistently shown that rigid fealty to Western masculine norms — such as prioritizing work, power-seeking and status — link with poor mental and physical health. Endorsement of such norms also correlates with misogynistic beliefs and violent behaviors, including sexual violence, studies have shown.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

But giving men a talking-to about their many defects rarely lands well. Nor does that negative focus help men thrive. But what approach would help? “We don’t really have a definition of men’s health. If we don’t know what we are going towards, how can we even do this [research]?” says Matt Englar-Carlson, a counseling expert at California State University, Fullerton.

What traits, the researchers wondered, define a healthy man? And could a healthy reframing of manhood improve men’s outcomes, such as by getting them to the doctor or lowering their high rates of social isolation, depression and even death by suicide?

Those questions would cleave the field, though as fights go, this one has been downright nice. McDermott, a psychologist of masculinity at the University of South Alabama in Mobile, would ultimately question positive masculinity’s very existence. Meanwhile, his friends and collaborators at Movember — a nonprofit research organization based in Richmond, Australia that encourages mustache-growing in November to spark conversations around men’s health issues — are poised for a 2027 launch of the Healthy Manhood Index. That scale uses a positive framing and is designed to gauge men’s strengths, while illuminating areas for improvement.

The first gender measurement scale emerged almost a century ago. It positioned femininity and masculinity at opposite poles, with researchers assuming that the most gender-conforming men and women were the healthiest.

That thinking has since unraveled. As women began smashing gender barriers, by doing everything from donning pants to entering the workforce, penalties for women acting more masculine largely disappeared.

Inspired by the feminist movement, researchers began studying the masculine psyche. Yet they largely framed masculinity as a barrier to health. The Male Role Norms Inventory, one of the most popular masculinity scales in use today, exemplifies that focus. Individuals rank statements like: “A man must stand on his own two feet and never depend on other people to help him do things.”

The higher the score on that and more than 60 similar statements appearing in popular masculinity scales used over the past 50 or so years, the worse men’s outcomes, McDermott and his colleagues at Movember reported in July in Men and Masculinities. “Manlier” men often struggle with depression and substance use and engage in sexual aggression. They also tend to avoid asking for help or taking precautionary health measures, such as wearing a mask during the COVID-19 pandemic.

But almost 80 percent of the statements used frame masculinity as a problem to be solved, the team found. That deficit lens biases the findings, argues coauthor and social psychologist Peter Fisher of the Movember Institute of Men’s Health, the organization’s research arm. “If the only tools you have available to you are looking for deficits, you will find deficits,” says Fisher, who is based in Santa Monica, Calif.

That negative framing has also seeped into public discourse, so much so that some people now intuitively link “masculinity” with the word “toxic.”

Yet those most macho of men are the outliers, the small percentage who score highest on masculinity scales, Englar-Carlson says. He suspects that what really matters for health is flexibility around when to behave in certain ways. Stoicism, a typically masculine-coded trait, can be calming in emergencies but scary when a man experiences a mental health crisis and refuses help.

Englar-Carlson and psychologist Mark Kiselica, of Penn State University, Harrisburg, developed the Positive Psychology Positive Masculinity, or PPPM, paradigm in 2010. Public health experts, therapists and others should focus on men’s strengths not deficits, they argued.

The ideas in PPPM are what McDermott began trying to turn into a masculinity scale a few years later. But his efforts sent him into a tailspin.

He and his colleagues began by identifying positive traits that people linked more with men than women. The team generated a list of 79 possible positive male attributes based on findings from focus groups and studies of positive masculinity and positive psychology, such as “having a good sense of humor,” “serving country or community” and “having passion for one’s work.” More than 1,000 individuals then rated those attributes on a scale from 1 for “strongly disagree” to 7 for “strongly agree” along three dimensions: positive, typically expected of men and typically expected of women.

Roughly 40 percent of the attributes, particularly those pertaining to protective behaviors and assertiveness, were seen as both positive and expected more of men than of women, McDermott and his colleagues reported in 2019 in Psychology of Men & Masculinities.

But the study also showed that both men and women scored above the midpoint on almost all the allegedly male attributes. That could mean the supposedly gendered attributes had little to do with gender. And for many measures, such as patience and having good hygiene, women scored higher than men. Could that mean that the study’s list was rebranding attributes from feminism as masculine? The idea didn’t sit well with McDermott.

Then, the team’s research took a dark turn. The researchers had respondents fill out both their new masculinity survey and a scale measuring sexist beliefs. That revealed that the more strongly respondents endorsed masculine ideals, the more likely they were to endorse sexist beliefs, the team’s unpublished work shows. Think about a statement like, “A good man should be strong,” McDermott says. For many people, that translates to “a good woman should be weak.”

“I’ve looked at this across three different samples [of people], and I find the same results each time,” McDermott says. “Whenever you define masculinity, you are inherently defining it against femininity.”

Most attributes are neither male nor female, but human, McDermott has come to believe. And gendering those universal traits merely reinforces sexist stereotypes. The work has left him gutted. “I really thought that there was such thing as positive masculinity,” he says. “But now I believe that it can never truly be positive.”

Fisher is well aware of McDermott’s journey. “He’s been trying to create a positive masculinity scale, or isolate the positive characteristics of masculinity, for a while,” Fisher says. “And he’s been struggling.”

Perhaps McDermott has set too high a bar, Fisher says. Rather than trying to identify and measure masculinity through beliefs, he says, why not focus on men’s actions?

So for the past several years, Fisher and colleagues have been doing just that. They have organized numerous focus groups and tested survey statements with some 12,000 individuals across six countries. Besides addressing the lack of age and cultural diversity used to create most masculinity scales currently in use, Fisher and his team hope that their scale will provide men with a blueprint for what constitutes healthy behavior.

Below are qualities Movember Institute of Men’s Health researchers are evaluating to develop a new masculinity scale. The items are preliminary and may not appear in the final version. The rows show counterproductive behaviors that result from pressures facing men, healthy responses and possible wording for survey statements the men would then rate.

All the statements in the Healthy Manhood Index start with “I” plus a verb, such as “I do,” “I talk” or “I check in,” Fisher says. For instance, men often feel pressure to restrict their emotions, so the healthy response would be for men to open up emotionally. The index might have men rate a statement like: “I share difficult things I’m going through with people I trust.” Crucially, the higher the score on the index, the healthier the man.

Fisher’s goal is to move men toward healthy behaviors without alienating them. “We just want to meet men where they are,” he says.

A debate that could easily become acrimonious has remained almost cloyingly friendly. McDermott refers to Fisher as “brilliant.” Fisher credits McDermott for “letting the data change his mind.”

Researchers in the field recognize that they share the same goals, says psychological researcher Michael Addis of Clark University in Worcester, Mass. They want men to be healthier and to treat others, including women and seemingly less masculine men, with respect. “The question is how do we do that? We either sell them on a new masculinity, or we say ‘…. masculinity is always going to be in some ways a box,’” he says.

Though discussions around how to frame masculinity can feel wonky, the stakes are real, Addis and psychiatrist and behavioral scientist Ethan Hoffmann of Stanford University wrote in 2024 in Psychology of Men & Masculinities.

Consider suicide. Men who strongly endorsed masculine norms were less likely than others to seek help for depression and more likely to die by suicide, researchers reported in 2025 in Psychiatry International.

Theoretically, public health campaigns aimed at men can help. But what form should they take? A positive masculinity campaign may recast a statement like, “real men never ask for help” to “real men know when it’s time to ask for help,” Addis and Hoffman write. But a campaign that rejects gender labels may roll out statements like: “Real men aren’t real: It’s a fiction that could cost you your life.”

Such postgender messaging may feel too abstract for the average guy, Fisher says. Convincing a 65-year-old man to stay on top of his prostate cancer appointments is hard enough without trying to shift his worldview.

McDermott counters that positive masculinity “makes the sex role stuff continue,” enshrining the idea that gender roles and hierarchies constitute a necessary organizing principle for societies.

Reconciliation may be possible, Addis says. Policy makers and public health experts could first rope men in with a more positive masculine approach. Then over time, they could help men question and relinquish gender norms. “I call it dancing with the devil,” or temporarily adopting the gendered approach as a means to a desired end, he says.

However the debate unfurls, researchers are writing their own script on how to fight like real men — or real people. “There’s a lot of men in the psychology of men [field] who have worked really hard to not let our egos get in the way of good work,” Addis says. “It’s sort of like practice what you preach.”

If you or someone you care about may be at risk of suicide, the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline offers free, 24/7 support, information and local resources from trained counselors. Call or text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org.
