#6179. Trump’s ‘invasion’ asylum ban to face justices

The border wall is seen in 2021 stretching along the U.S.-Mexico border near Columbus, N.M. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

The Supreme Court agreed on Friday to hear a challenge to President Donald Trump’s claims that an “invasion” at the southern border can be used to deny asylum claims by refugees.

The Trump administration had asked the justices to review a decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit that held the president could not broadly deny asylum claims under federal law. The case is the latest high-profile fight over one of Trump’s signature domestic policies.

The administration argues in its petition for the justices to take the case that the president has broad authority over asylum claims, which includes shutting down the system entirely because he has decided he will not grant any.

“The proclamation thus lawfully suspends access to asylum, which is a purely discretionary benefit. The court of appeals’ insistence that aliens are entitled to file futile asylum applications elevates empty procedures over substance,” the petition says.

Trump issued the order on his first day in office, declaring an “invasion” on the southern border and using that as a reason to deny asylum claims by refugees who present themselves there. The order is still in place, preventing asylum claims at the U.S.-Mexico border while the lawsuit plays out.

In court filings asking the justices to take the case, the administration pointed to “dramatic” reductions in illegal border crossings, which freed up resources to combat human trafficking and other threats.

In Friday’s order, the justices agreed to hear arguments over the legality of Trump’s executive order as well as whether the lower-court judge could grant an order in favor of all asylum seekers rather than just the ones who brought the suit.

Immigration rights groups initially challenged the order and won a successful ruling from a federal judge in Washington. The administration later appealed to the D.C. Circuit, where it lost at a three-judge panel before it brought the case before the justices.

The D.C. Circuit held that although federal law provides a president discretion in denying asylum claims, he cannot do so categorically.

The ACLU and immigrant rights groups who brought the case defended the ruling in their own filing. The filing argues that Congress mandated the creation of the asylum system and the president “may not invent by fiat a new removal system that eviscerates the protections Congress mandated by statute.”

Last term the justices ruled in favor of a separate policy dating to the first Trump administration that allowed officials to prevent asylum claims by stopping refugees from actually reaching the U.S. border.

A ruling in favor of the refugees could allow the administration to restart that policy and still deny asylum claims.

The case granted Friday is the latest high-profile immigration policy clash on the justices’ docket this term. Earlier this year the justices agreed to hear a challenge to the administration’s policy that most immigrants facing deportation should be detained without bond.

The justices will likely hear oral arguments and decide the case granted Friday before the end of the court’s term next June.

The case is Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services.

#6177. Conservative firebrand Lauren Boebert ousted in Colorado

Rep. Lauren Boebert, R-Colo., leaves the Capitol after a vote on Wednesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

Colorado Rep. Lauren Boebert, an outspoken conservative and Second Amendment provocateur, lost her bid for a fourth term to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, a retired rear admiral in the Navy.

Laubacher was leading 48.8 percent to 47.9 percent, a margin of 3,441 votes, when The Associated Press called the race on Friday.

The red-hued 4th District, which spreads across eastern Colorado, was unexpectedly competitive this year, a sign of how deep into red turf Democrats were able to compete this year. Boebert had Donald Trump’s endorsement, but her relationship with the president has been strained at times after she began pressing for the release of files related to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

Laubacher proved to be a strong fundraiser, hauling in $13.7 million as of mid-October to Boebert’s $1.2 million.

Boebert has been one of the most visible and controversial members of the House GOP conference since she won an upset primary in the 3rd District over five-term incumbent Republican Scott Tipton in 2020.

A newcomer to electoral politics, she quickly positioned herself as a disruptor on Capitol Hill, heckling former President Joe Biden during his 2022 State of the Union address and tangling with a fellow GOP firebrand, former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene of Georgia, on the House floor.

In 2023, Boebert was embroiled in an embarrassing incident in a Denver theater that was captured on surveillance video. She subsequently embarked on an apology tour.

Running for reelection the first time in the 3rd District, which is centered around Colorado’s rural Western Slope, Boebert barely won a closer-than-expected race against Democrat Adam Frisch in 2022. When Frisch announced he was trying again in 2024, Boebert switched to the 4th District, which had been considered far friendlier terrain for the GOP.

This year, Democrats won all of Colorado’s House seats, except in the 3rd District, which is held by Rep. Jeff Hurd.

Mary Ellen McIntire contributed to this report.

#6176. Norse Atlantic Says Financial Situation ‘Critical’

After close to a year of dire financial warnings, Norway’s Norse Atlantic Airways said Wednesday that its situation is “critical” and that it must obtain short-term financing to continue operations.

The Arendal-based carrier has struggled with higher jet fuel prices brought on by the war in Iran and the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. In the months since the war started, the airline has cut staff, furloughed some crew members, suspended unprofitable routes, and instituted temporary pay reductions for some non-flying crew, but these steps have apparently not put Norse Atlantic back on solid ground.

“[The company’s financial condition is] dependent on securing financing to meet its short term liquidity needs and to continue its operations,” officials said in a statement. “Norse, supported by its advisors, has explored various strategic alternatives and entertains discussions for a potential takeover.”

“Norse is also engaged in discussions with selected parties on short term financing, however, there can be no assurances that such discussions will result in a viable solution,” the message continued. “Norse will provide further information as and when appropriate.”

Rising fuel costs have set back airlines around the world, but the squeeze is arguably worst in Europe, since the continent depends mainly on Gulf oil and has little domestic refining capacity. The crisis has forced Latvia’s airBaltic into bankruptcy, teed up EasyJet’s sale to Apollo Global Management, and inflicted considerable damage on Lufthansa’s core brand.

It was not immediately clear if Norse Atlantic has any candidates in mind for a potential merger. The carrier is not part of any global airline alliance, though it partners with operators such as EasyJet, Norwegian Air Shuttle, and Pegasus through its Norse Connections program.

Bloomberg reported in 2023 and 2024 that the carrier was weighing alliances with larger airlines, possibly through an equity stake, but none were named.

Norse Atlantic operates only long-haul flights. Its network has been adjusted multiple times over the last year in an effort to reduce costs.

#6171. Former Washington Rep. Jim McDermott dies at 89

Former Rep. Jim McDermott, D-Wash., is seen in a vineyard near his cottage in Civrac-en-Médoc, France, on March 20, 2024. (Ariel Cohen/CQ Roll Call)

Former Rep. Jim McDermott, D-Wash., a fierce advocate for universal health care and outspoken war critic who served 28 years in Congress, died Thursday at the age of 89, his family announced.

In a roughly 50-year career in state and federal office, the salty-tongued, liberal lawmaker from Seattle won both praise and criticism for pushing an aggressive agenda focused on expanding health care to all Americans.

As the top Democrat on the House Ways and Means Health Subcommittee, McDermott defended the 2010 Affordable Care Act that expanded health insurance to millions of Americans, while critics complained it did little to control costs.

“Jim was one of the first and most powerful voices fighting to fix our broken health care system in Congress,” Sen. Patty Murray, D-Wash., wrote on X. “He was passionate and fearless — and left a tremendous legacy on WA state and its people. My thoughts are with Congressman McDermott’s family and loved ones during this difficult time.”

When McDermott announced his retirement from Congress in 2016, then-President Barack Obama praised him in a statement as “a much-needed voice for his most vulnerable constituents.”

Born and raised in Illinois, McDermott came from a poor, conservative and deeply religious family. His father, a bond underwriter, and his mother, a telephone operator and homemaker, started a church in the garage of their two-bedroom home. His three siblings slept in one bedroom; his parents in the other. McDermott, the oldest child, had the couch.

He attended the conservative evangelical Wheaton College. His bend toward liberalism began during medical school at the University of Illinois, when he voted for John F. Kennedy in the 1960 presidential election. After a stint in the U.S. Navy Medical Corps from 1968-1970, McDermott won his first seat in the Washington state House in 1970 running on an anti-war platform.

He continued his anti-war stances in Congress, voting against the 2002 resolution authorizing the use of military force in Iraq. In 2013, he opposed U.S. intervention in Syria and was one of only 20 House members to vote against new sanctions on Iran.

Shortly after he retired from Congress, McDermott settled on a new life for himself by moving to a small town in southwestern France, where he admired some of the public policies he had fought hard to deliver in Washington with mixed success.

“I spent 16 years in the Washington state legislature trying to get single-payer health care,” he recalled in a 2024 interview with CQ Roll Call at his home about 90 minutes outside of Bourdeaux. “Then I spent nearly 30 years in Congress trying to get single-payer. Then I came to France and in three months I had single-payer. Was that mind-blowing? You bet.”

As he said, McDermott dedicated much time in the Washington state legislature to trying to create a single-payer system. When that didn’t work out, he developed the Washington State Basic Health Program, a health coverage system for the unemployed and working poor — the first state program of its kind.

Then, once he got to Washington, he tried to work with then-First Lady Hillary Clinton to hatch a federal single-payer program, but that effort came to naught. He later backed the Affordable Care Act and tried to pass his own legislation in 2015 for comprehensive health care coverage.

“The only way to truly ensure that access to quality health care is a right enjoyed by every American is through a single-payer system,” he said in a statement at the time.

McDermott will also be remembered for some of the attacks he leveled against Republicans. In the most notorious incident, he was ordered to pay then-Rep. John A. Boehner of Ohio — who later became speaker — nearly $1.1 million in 2008 after releasing a recording of a 1996 cell phone call between Boehner and then-Speaker Newt Gingrich. McDermott maintained it was worth the fight, and the cost of the settlement, to protect free speech.

“Jim McDermott was as big as it gets in Washington state politics,” Sen. Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., wrote on Facebook. “Smart, funny, and Irish, Jim McDermott will be missed.”

Is Norwegian Luna the best big new ship sailing out of Miami?

For someone looking for a vessel that feels more refined and upscale than what is typical among big Miami-based ships, it just might be.

As I saw during a week on board in October, Norwegian Luna has an elevated design compared to many of the big new ships sailing out of Miami, giving it an elegance that stands out among the competition.

That said, for someone who just wants the widest array of onboard amusements, entertainment and nightlife that they can find on a cruise ship, the choice gets harder.

Although its large, the eight-month-old Norwegian Luna — the latest in Norwegian Cruise Line's Prima Plus class — is notably smaller than the other big new ships that it is up against in Miami. That means there's less room for the wide range of attractions you'll find on those vessels.

Unlike two of its biggest rivals in the market, Royal Caribbean's Icon of the Seas and MSC Cruises' MSC World America, for instance, it lacks a water park area with multiple waterslides on its top deck (though it does have one large water attraction, the Aqua Slidecoaster). It also has fewer and smaller main pool areas. That's a real strike against it for families with kids, in particular.

As someone who generally prefers more intimate and elegant ships, I know which side of the trade-off I'm on. If it were my money, I'd lean toward Norwegian Luna. It's the perfect big ship for me.

But read on to see if it's right for you.

Unveiled in March, Norwegian Luna is the second ship in Norwegian's new Prima Plus Class of vessels, following the slightly older Norwegian Aqua (the latter also sails from Miami, so any ranking of the best new ships sailing from the city would rightly list the two ships in a virtual tie).

These two ships, along with two similar but slightly smaller Prima Class vessels that debuted in 2022 and 2023, are smaller than the ships that Norwegian launched just before them, which is a bit unusual. Most of Norwegian's competitors, such as Royal Caribbean and MSC Cruises, have been rolling out ever bigger ships, loaded with ever more onboard attractions and venues.

Related: Norwegian Cruise Line ships ranked from biggest to smallest

For now, Norwegian Luna mostly operates seven-night voyages to the Caribbean out of Miami on Saturdays, competing head-to-head with new ships from Royal Caribbean and MSC Cruises (Icon of the Seas and MSC World America) that are much bigger.

Those two ships, notably, are 59% and 38% bigger than Luna, respectively, allowing for a lot more onboard venues of all kinds, from decktop attractions to showrooms, restaurants and bars.

On the flip side, Norwegian Luna's smaller size, coupled with its elevated design, generally contributes to a more intimate and elegant feel — a significant differentiator.

I say "generally," as Norwegian Luna's more elegant feel is sometimes punctured by aggressive upselling and extra charges that are incongruous with the ship's overall vibe.

It's not a dealbreaker, but it's off-putting at times and something you need to be prepared for going into a sailing.

Cabins are a strong point on Norwegian Luna. The majority of balcony cabins (the biggest category of cabins on the ship) are surprisingly spacious at 358 square feet, with a clean-lined, modern design and solid storage. I particularly love the bathrooms, which offer larger showers than you sometimes get on mass-market ships as well as a clever pivot door that makes them easy to enter.

Balcony cabins account for about 57% of Norwegian Luna's 1,813 cabins. But there are also 140 oceanview cabins without balconies of various sizes and 424 windowless "inside" cabins that offer a modern design with solid storage.

The latter category includes 73 very small but perfect-for-one solo cabins, known as Studios, in a keycard-access-only solo area with its own lounge — a Norwegian signature. Norwegian has leaned into the solo cruise market in recent years with these exclusive solo areas, and the cabins are in high demand. Book one early if you want one.

Norwegian Luna is also home to one of the line's signature The Haven suite complexes. These are separate, keycard-access-only enclaves found on many Norwegian ships that not only have a wide range of lovely suites but also their own private restaurants, lounges and bars, and outdoor sun and pool decks.

On Norwegian Luna, this complex (tied with the one on Norwegian Aqua as the biggest in the fleet) fills the top four decks of the back of the ship, accessible via its own private elevator. It's truly wonderful. Staying in one of its suites — there are 123, including 25 Owner's Suites that measure up to an astounding 2,100 square feet — feels like staying in a completely different, far more upscale vessel.

Among my favorite features of Norwegian Luna's Haven area is its cozy bar, which offers a much-upgraded bar experience to what you'll find anywhere else on the ship. There are higher-end spirits and creative craft cocktails made by some of the best bartenders at sea.

In addition to the suites in The Haven, you'll find additional suites and penthouses outside the area that also come with extra privileges but not all the perks that Haven guests receive.

Pro tip: If you are sensitive to noise, steer clear of cabins with connecting doors to adjacent cabins (you'll find them noted on Norwegian Luna's deck plans). Even when closed, their imperfect seals will cause you to hear noise from the cabin next door.

Norwegian ships have always been known for a wide range of restaurant choices, and Norwegian Luna is no exception. It has more than a dozen sit-down eateries, ranging from a super-casual food hall to a high-end steakhouse — some quite good for a big, mass-market ship.

Just be warned that the restaurant scene on Norwegian Luna is one of the areas where you'll encounter a lot of upcharges, with both high cover charges for some restaurants and additional charges for individual menu items that can really push up the bill.

Among the priciest eateries on board are Norwegian's two signature restaurants, Cagney's Steakhouse (found on every Norwegian ship) and the French-focused Le Bistro (found on nearly every Norwegian ship). Both have cover charges of $60 per person that rise to $72 per person with a mandatory 20% gratuity; that price can climb even higher if you order an item with an upcharge.

Both are elegant and upscale, and serve quality dishes, as does Palomar, which serves seafood-focused Mediterranean cuisine for the same $60 cover charge. I highly recommend Palomar's whole fish-for-two baked in salt, which is well worth its additional $25 charge ($30 with the mandatory gratuity) — not just because it's a showy dish that tastes as good as it looks, but because it's deboned tableside, adding some tableside theatrics to the evening.

Other extra-charge eateries include Los Lobos ($40 per person), which dishes out Mexican cuisine; Nama Sushi & Sashimi ($50 per person), for its namesake Japanese cuisine; Japanese hibachi restaurant Hasuki ($60 per person); and Thai-centered Sukothai ($50 per person).

All of these have mandatory 20% gratuity charges on top of their cover charges, as does Onda by Scarpetta, which is an Italian eatery ($40 per person) with ties to New York City's high-end Scarpetta restaurant. The latter is one eatery I'd skip, as the cuisine is spotty and the service more rushed than relaxing. (Despite ordering four courses, we were barely there an hour as the dishes were raced out to us one on top of the other.)

For those keeping to a tight budget, there are fortunately plenty of solid included-in-the-fare options on Norwegian Luna, too.

The real standout here is Indulge Food Hall, a casual, multi-outlet venue with separate stands and counters serving tapas, Indian dishes, noodles, vegetarian bowls, barbecue, Latin and Mexican food, and rotisserie items. Some of these items, particularly the Indian dishes (which include chicken tikka made in an actual tandoor oven), are quite good for a free-on-a-ship casual eatery.

Pro tip: If you're sitting at one of the many tables scattered around Indulge Food Hall, you can order from any of the stands and counters via a tabletop tablet. But if you sit at the counter for any particular food outlet, you can only order from that outlet's menu. Pick your seats with that in mind.

A sleeper hit with no extra charge is The Local Bar and Grill, which has both indoor and outdoor seating with a casual diner vibe. It's open around the clock for table-served American comfort food (think: burgers, chicken wings and nachos). But most importantly, for me, it's a calmer and less crowded place for breakfast than the seemingly always-jammed buffet at the top of the ship (more on that in a moment). I loved sitting in its outdoor area on sea days, overlooking the water, for a leisurely eggs-bacon-and-toast breakfast served by a friendly waiter — a much more civilized experience than the buffet.

By contrast, the shiptop buffet called Surfside is an included-in-the-fare outlet to avoid. While a convenient quick-bite option for passengers lounging at the pool (it's right next door), it's too small for a ship the size of Norwegian Luna. It has too few tables, too few food stations and too narrow a walkway along the food stations to be a pleasant experience much of the time it's open.

Rounding out the included-in-the-fare options are two larger complimentary sit-down restaurants, The Commodore Room and Hudson's. Both offer the same dinner menu, with decent, if not always consistent, offerings and pleasant service. Hudson's is also open for breakfast and lunch.

Among the upcharges at both eateries are $20-$30 fees for signature dishes from the ship's Cagney's Steakhouse, such as its ribeye steak ($25). While I'm generally not a fan of the trend toward more upcharges at supposedly included-in-the-fare cruise ship eateries, this does allow for what is one of my favorite dining hacks when sailing on a Norwegian ship: creating an almost-as-good-as-the-real-thing Cagney's steakhouse experience at less than half the price.

I order that ribeye and the always-available Caesar salad (nearly identical to the one at Cagney's except you don't get anchovies on top) and a couple of glasses of the included-in-Free-at-Sea-packages Malbec, which is the very same Malbec offered at Cagney's, and pretend I'm at the latter eatery. The total cost, including the mandatory gratuity, is $30 versus $72 per person at Cagney's.

No matter where you are on Norwegian Luna, you are never far from a bar. There are more than a dozen of them in the interior parts of the ship alone, plus more on the outside decks.

Among the liveliest (and my personal favorite) is the Metropolitan Bar, which stands out for its "zero waste" cocktails featuring such ingredients as syrup made from discarded banana peels. It's bustling every night with live music that ranges from Latin beats to classic '80s rock.

The Belvedere Bar at the top level of the atrium is also hopping with live music nightly, as is the Penrose Bar two decks below. (Musicians play at the base of the atrium not far from it.)

All three of these bars line high-traffic areas and can get busy. For something more tucked away, quieter and usually less crowded, the side-by-side Whiskey Bar and Swirl Wine Bar offer intimate spaces dedicated strictly to their respective namesake pours.

There's also the bar at The Local Bar & Grill mentioned in the restaurant section above, which serves as the casual go-to spot to catch a game over bar bites.

Beyond these, you'll find multiple bars servicing the pool and activity areas at the top of the ship as well as every interior entertainment venue, including the main theater and comedy club. Up at the very front of the ship, the Observation Lounge pairs a full bar with sweeping daytime ocean views.

What you won't find on Norwegian Luna, unlike on some competitor ships sailing from Miami, is a true craft cocktail venue. The Metropolitan Bar comes the closest with its "zero waste" cocktails. But even here, most drinks are quick-made affairs lacking the house-made ingredients, specialty clear ice and precision construction that has become commonplace at craft bars on land.

The Whiskey Bar also has craft elements, including a wide range of whiskeys and knowledgeable bartenders mixing old fashioneds, Boulevardiers and other whiskey drinks with precision. But the venue falls down on things like proper ice for drinks. (They oddly have just 20 large cubes available each night, which disappear fast, resulting in most cocktails coming out with the same small ice cubes found at the basic bars on the pool deck.)

For coffee drinkers, a full-size Starbucks in the atrium rounds out the beverage options.

Norwegian is no longer the leader in big ship entertainment, following cutbacks over the past three years. All the big-name Broadway shows, from "Jersey Boys" to "Kinky Boots," are gone. But it still offers solid entertainment in its main theaters, including the one on Norwegian Luna.

The big crowdpleaser on Norwegian Luna is "Elton: A Celebration of Elton John," a flashy tribute show that strings together John's biggest hits with visual pizzazz that includes elaborate costumes and choreography, special effects and archival footage projected on a back screen. If you're an Elton John fan like me, you'll love it.

The other big show in the Luna Theater, "HIKO: Innovation Meets Wonder," is a moody, sci-fi-themed mashup of custom-scored music, dance, showy costumes, 3D projections, lasers and acrobatics (think high-flying trampoline acts and aerial silk routines). It starts out slow but picks up toward the end.

There's also a rocking Eagles tribute show in the main theater with a full band, which is another crowd-pleaser. There are also more tribute shows focused on Billy Joel and Fleetwood Mac (the former in the smaller Syd Norman Pour House; the latter at the main theater).

And yes, you'll see a theme among the performers Norwegian has chosen for these tribute shows. These are all musical groups that are popular with Baby Boomers and Generation Xers who grew up with them, but have also had a resurgence among younger generations — perfect for Norwegian's wide demographic.

One other notable entertainment option is LunaTique Pop Circus, a bawdy, adults-only, cabaret-style nightlife experience set to pop music, with plenty of audience participation. (If the idea of being pulled up on stage terrifies you, don't sit in the front rows.) It's the only show on Norwegian Luna with an extra charge ($45 per person, including four drinks that get served to everyone as part of the show).

LunaTique Pop Circus takes place in Improv at Sea, an intimate comedy club that also is the place for stand-up comedy on most nights.

While not quite as elaborate as the entertainment on the larger Royal Caribbean and MSC Cruises ships that sail out of Miami on weekends, the above shows have been earning high marks from cruisers since Norwegian Luna debuted and are among the most popular activities on the ship.

Just be warned that, because of that popularity, it can sometimes be hard to get a seat for these shows, which is a common complaint among passengers. With just 752 seats, the Luna Theater is small for a ship the size of Norwegian Luna and fills up long before showtime. Ditto for the smaller Syd Norman's Pour House and Improv at Sea venues, which each can hold just 100 or so people.

If you want a seat for any of the shows, particularly a good seat near the front, head to the venue at least 45 minutes in advance.

Norwegian Luna has a lot to offer on its top decks, particularly in the "family fun" department.

The standout attraction is its giant Aqua Slidecoaster water ride. It uses the same magnetic accelerator system found in modern roller coasters to blast you skyward in a raft that then takes you winding back down a meandering waterslide course. It's both tons of fun and completely free.

You'll find several more fun family attractions tucked under and around the Aqua Slidecoaster, including a 12-hole, high-tech minigolf course where each stroke of your ball is electronically tracked and you get bonus points for hitting certain targets. It comes with a per-person charge of $5 but is well worth it.

Also in this area is The Stadium (free outdoor games including table tennis, bean bag toss and foosball) and the Bull's Eye Bar, which features tech-enhanced darts games.

You'll also find the entrance to The Drop, a terrifying-looking dry slide that spirals 10 decks down the side of the ship. It was a hard pass for me, but try it if you're daring.

Rounding out this area are a pickleball court and Glow Court — a high-tech sports court with an LED wall that lets you play challenging ball-throwing games (just be careful not to hit your partner with a ball, as I did; you might find yourself in the doghouse).

While great fun, these attractions eat up a lot of real estate on the top decks, leaving less room for pool areas. The ship's main pool area, just in front of the Aqua Slidecoaster, feels small for a ship the size of Norwegian Luna (and, indeed, was uncomfortably jammed on sea days during my sailing).

One deck up from the pool is the often-crowded Kids' Aqua Park, where little ones can enjoy water sprayers and mini waterslides.

The solution to escape the crowds (if you're kid-free, at least) is to spend $289 per person for a weekly pass to the adults-only Vibe Beach Club — a separate, keycard-access-only deck-top lounge area that is roughly the same size as the main pool area but limited to just 166 passengers. It is blissfully uncrowded and quiet compared to the main pool area and has its own bar and hot tubs facing the sea.

Pro tip: Splurge for one of the 12 private cabanas at the Vibe Beach Club, which cost a seemingly high $619 per week but come with access for two people, so they're really only about $310 per person. That's just $21 more per person than buying two Vibe passes, and it's a much nicer experience.

Alternatively, you can book a cabin in The Haven, which, as noted above, also has its own decktop lounge area (at the back of the ship) with its own pool and bar.

Between these two areas (Vibe and The Haven), Norwegian Luna notably has a lot more of its decktop real estate devoted to exclusive upcharge areas than other big ships sailing from Miami. What this effectively means is that the ship offers a bifurcated decktop experience. If you pay up, you will experience something more relaxing and exclusive than you will find on many other big ships. If you don't, the top deck experience might feel less appealing.

That said, if you're willing to head down nine decks, you'll find additional outdoor lounge space with lounge chairs and small plunge pools along an outdoor promenade that wraps around the sides of the ships. With a cool South Beach vibe that includes plush circular seats for two surrounded by wading pools, it's an innovative additional outdoor area that is often less crowded than the top-deck pool area.

For indoor fun, the family-focused Luna Game Zone near the Observation Lounge offers an array of video, virtual reality and other games (some for free and some for a fee). Plus, for adults, there's a sizable casino with VIP and smoking rooms, as well as slots and table games.

Norwegian Luna also has a massive, multilevel spa (the Mandara Spa) with one of the loveliest and most relaxing thermal suites at sea. Accessible for an extra charge, it has a stunning, two-deck-high room with water therapy pools; a separate area that is home to all sorts of therapeutic rooms including Finnish, charcoal and clay saunas, a steam room and a salt room; and a separate, blissfully relaxing room full of heated loungers overlooking the sea.

Just be warned that access to the thermal suite costs a sky-high $630 per person for the week (though discounts are sometimes available onboard at the start of the cruise).

The spa area is also where you'll find the ship's fitness room, which is free to use and offers plenty of cardio equipment and free weights, but lacks a full range of weight machines.

The ship's entertainment staff also programs all sorts of daily activities throughout the ship, including trivia games, karaoke, art and dance classes, and family events.

Through at least April 2028, Norwegian Luna will mostly sail seven-night cruises from Miami to the Caribbean, with departures on Saturdays. The exception is during the summer of 2027, when it will reposition to New York for four-, five- and seven-night cruises to Bermuda.

When sailing from Miami, the ship operates both Eastern and Western Caribbean itineraries. Eastern Caribbean itineraries typically include stops at Puerto Plata, Dominican Republic; St. Thomas, U.S. Virgin Islands; Tortola, British Virgin Islands; and Great Stirrup Cay, Norwegian's private island in the Bahamas. Western Caribbean itineraries typically bring calls in Roatan, Honduras; Harvest Caye, Belize; and Costa Maya and Cozumel, Mexico.

Related: Eastern Caribbean vs. Western Caribbean cruises

Fares for seven-night Caribbean sailings start at $549 per person, based on double occupancy. Fares for seven-night Bermuda sailings start at $1,229 per person, based on double occupancy.

Such pricing is for inside cabins on the most offseason dates. You'll pay more for oceanview and balcony cabins and suites, as well as for sailings on more in-demand weeks.

Norwegian Luna is a big new ship that feels more refined and upscale than many of the other big new ships sailing out of Miami. That's in part because of its more elegant design and its (relatively) smaller size. The downside of that smaller size is that the ship doesn't have quite as many onboard attractions — like decktop features, showrooms, restaurants and bars — as some of its competitors.

#6167. Trump administration ups ante on aviation funds after ground stop

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy leaves a House Republican Conference meeting in the Capitol on July 21. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Top administration officials doubled down on calls for Congress to supply additional funds for an ongoing air traffic modernization effort after they said old equipment contributed to the need for a nationwide ground stop of flights on Friday.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin increased their ask to $50 billion on Friday night, a day after Duffy and White House budget chief Russ Vought formally requested $30.1 billion.

The increased allotment, which the administration officials didn’t fully flesh out, comes after the nation’s air traffic control system experienced “instability” in its radar and communications at certain facilities earlier in the day, Duffy told reporters.

He said “inconsistency in the data” being issued by those systems led to implementation of the nationwide ground stop, saying the order was given out of “an abundance of caution” before being lifted about four hours later.

During a Friday night White House briefing, Duffy and Mullin explained the issues were driven by “an incredibly old air traffic control system.”

Earlier in the day, the stoppage had caused mass confusion and raised questions about potential terror attacks, or artificial intelligence breakouts resulting from new software the agency is rolling out. While Mullin said “we’re not ruling out anything,” he explained that “the public was never at danger through this process.”

Still, Duffy called the incident “an emergency” while calling for additional modernization funds.

“This is an emergency,” he said. “I want $50 billion. President Trump is a builder. He’s going to build this network and deliver for the American people. But the president can’t deliver for America unless the Congress delivers the money to make it happen.”

The latest figure is $19.1 billion higher than the figure Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought called on congressional appropriators to approve in a Thursday letter.

Mullin said the new $50 billion figure was an administration estimate for a “complete overhaul of the system” which has been going through a “patchwork” upgrade process that may have overwhelmed the older equipment still being used.

“We need someone to come in and build the whole system," Mullin said. "Nickel and diming it together does not work."

Thursday’s call for $30.1 billion echoes a White House-backed bill that Sen. Eric Schmitt, R-Mo., introduced in September, which would provide $10.1 billion for air traffic control upgrades, including $2 billion for "cloud computing and national airspace system telecommunications."

Those funds would come after $12.5 billion allocated to the effort through the July 2025 reconciliation law that Duffy and Vought called a “down-payment."

Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee Republicans touted those already-appropriated funds in a social media post. They pointed to $1.9 billion provided in the reconciliation law that would go toward upgrading air route traffic control centers, which guide planes across long distances after departure and which the FAA had cited as the cause of the problem.

The 22 air route traffic control centers across the country guide aircraft using instrument-dependent flight plans. Under such plans, pilots use instruments, electronic navigation and air traffic control assistance to guide them and maintain separation from other aircraft in certain airspaces.

The committee’s majority said Friday's outage highlighted the need to prioritize modernization of the air route traffic control centers, arguing that President Lyndon B. Johnson was in office the last time a new one was built.

Commerce ranking member Maria Cantwell, D-Wash., said in a statement Friday night that the panel is looking into FAA and airspace telecommunications issues.

“Technology issues related to how planes communicate through primary frequencies, backup frequencies, and other issues will be something the Commerce Committee will be reviewing,” Cantwell said.

Cantwell is poised to take the committee's gavel come January as Democrats assume the majority in the Senate.

In a joint statement Friday night, House Transportation and Infrastructure Chairman Sam Graves, R-Mo., and ranking member Rick Larsen, D-Wash., called the communication failures “concerning” and said their committee would “thoroughly review the issues that led to this nationwide ground stop.”

Both committees have also been in monthslong negotiations over dueling aviation safety bills responding to the January 2025 midair collision near Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport that killed 67 people.

At issue in those negotiations is which location transmission technology should be mandated to aid in air traffic control operations and allow aircraft to maintain appropriate distance. Leaders have said they hope to reach a deal in the lame-duck session.

#6162. China Southern Orders 50 737 MAX Jets

A subsidiary of China Southern Airlines has agreed to buy 50 Boeing 737 MAX 8 aircraft, Reuters reported Tuesday.

The airplanes, which have a total list price of $7.4 billion, will be used by Xiamen Airlines, which is based in Fujian. Deliveries are expected from 2031 to 2034.

The deal is Boeing’s largest with a Chinese operator in nearly a decade. The country largely shifted toward Airbus aircraft as relations with the U.S. frayed.

President Donald Trump hoped to reverse that trend during his state visit to China in May. Trump discussed a potential purchase directly with Chinese President Xi Jinping, and even brought along Boeing CEO Kelly Ortberg for the summit. Ultimately, Beijing agreed to buy 200 aircraft from Boeing, fewer than analysts expected, but still notable considering Boeing’s drought in the country.

Trump said earlier this week that he thinks China will buy 250 more aircraft from Boeing. He did not provide details or say where that information came from.

China Southern said the new aircraft will help Xiamen expand after it relocates to the new Xiamen Xiang’an International Airport. The facility will replace Xiamen Gaoqi International Airport as Xiamen’s main gateway.

Whether you’re taking a bucket-list trip to Doha or want to jazz up an annual vacation to Paris, Qatar Airways lets you enhance what can sometimes be the most stressful and dreary part of travel. Below, find all the best promo codes and coupons to help you save while enjoying the high life this Black Friday weekend.

Hurry, these Black Friday sales won't last long: Through end of day November 29 (11:59pm ET), find economy and business class flights up to 25% off for travel through October 31, 2027. Flights purchased in the sale are flexible too, with one free date change if needed. As for the fine print, there are some blackout dates, and the minimum stay is seven days.

Beyond the Cyber Week discounts, you can find Qatar Airways flash sales directly on the website, which run on and off throughout the year. You’ll need to catch them at just the right time (subscribing to the newsletter will help ensure you don’t miss any updates), since, due to their nature, they’re gone in a flash. The current sale is offering up to 15% off fares for flights to 170+ destinations for trips occurring through March 22, 2027. But you’ll have to book quickly since flash sales come and go in the blink of an eye.

Are you a student between the ages of 18 and 30 enrolled at an accredited college or university? Expect a plethora of spectacular benefits you’ll want to take advantage of, including complimentary Wi-Fi in the sky, extra baggage allowance (22 pounds of additional luggage, or an extra bag, depending on your route—especially helpful for beginning or end of semester flights), and an upgrade to a higher Privilege Club tier if you fly as a Student Club member at least once a year. Perhaps the most exciting benefit of all (especially for those of us, like me, who are no longer students), those enrolled in the Student Club can invite up to three family members or friends to be Student Companions, so they’ll share all of the Student Club benefits on their trip.

Join the Privilege Club, Qatar Airways's loyalty program, to rake in tons of benefits. Those who join now can use the code PCAMER26 by December 31, 2026, to earn up to 4,000 bonus Avios (Qatar Airways’s rewards currency) to use on upcoming flights, upgrades, and extra baggage allowances. Travelers will receive their Avios directly in their online account after their first flight as a member, as long as they remember to include their membership number when booking their original flight. Mendocino, a small coastal town in northern California, has welcomed its first points property. The nearly 50-year-old Hill House hotel was renovated and reopened in June 2026 as Hill House at Trailborn Mendocino, Outdoor Collection by Marriott Bonvoy — making it the first and only member of a major hotel loyalty program in Mendocino proper. (The closest options are members of IHG One Rewards and Wyndham Rewards in neighboring Fort Bragg.)

The Mendocino Coast region is known for its charming small-town vibes, natural beauty and outdoor pursuits, so the Trailborn brand’s laidback nature lodge concept fits in here like a seal in nearby Mendocino Bay. I stayed three nights in late October to get a first look at the property (and the town, which is on TPG’s 2027 Where to Go list).

Nestled just a few minutes’ walk outside downtown Mendocino, Hill House at Trailborn Mendocino’s unassuming two-story buildings fit right in with the surrounding hotel scene. The design is inspired by nature — specifically, the redwood forests and tide pools of the surrounding Mendocino Coast — while still feeling modern and polished.

The grounds are bursting with native plants, many of them still in bloom when I visited in late October. Botanical art prints and zoological illustrations on the walls give a nod to the great outdoors, and curious guests can lose themselves in the lobby’s curiosity cabinet, a revamped relic of the original building. Visitors are encouraged to sign the guestbook with a stamp of a dried leaf or flower.

The hotel offers just 44 accommodations — relatively large for a Mendocino property — including 14 double queen rooms, 25 king rooms and 5 junior suites. Within each room type, travelers can choose to upgrade to features such as a balcony or deck, an ocean view or both.

My room, a spacious King Junior Suite Ocean View, felt like a relaxing retreat with its muted color palette of greens, browns and yellows and its cozy linen spa robes. After a day of exploring Mendocino, I enjoyed relaxing on the sofa, perusing the coffee table book Botanicum, and sampling locally made goodies from the snack basket and minibar (for a fee).

Trailborn Hill House has one on-site restaurant: Pizza Standard Time, a casual bar and diner offering mostly pizza, plus salads, charcuterie boards and small Italian bites like arancini. The fare was limited but tasty; my friend and I tried a pizza, salad, and local Husch chardonnay and were quite happy. It’s nice having a quick, casual meal available on-site in case you arrive late and tired from the drive, but it’s also just a few minutes’ walk to Mendocino if you want more options.

Like all Trailborn properties, this one offers a lobby convenience store called Hill House Wine & Grocer. Guests can purchase local drinks and snacks (mostly the kind you’d find on a charcuterie board), plus apparel, toys, candles with the property’s signature scent and other souvenirs.

The hotel also offered a small but delicious complimentary breakfast spread. As with everything else during my stay, the breakfast was high-quality yet unpretentious, with guests serving and bussing their own tables. Instead of having a designated breakfast area, guests can find a cozy spot to eat inside Pizza Standard Time or the attached Cabot Cove Detective Library, outside by one of the fire pits or back to their room.

However, this will change when Trailborn’s second Mendocino property, The Mendocino Hotel, opens in 2027. Instead of complimentary breakfast, Hill House plans to provide guests with a voucher to Moonwave, The Mendocino Hotel’s dining concept, which will serve “coastal comfort” food three meals a day plus drinks at the lobby bar.

If you didn’t realize you were in a small town, you will as soon as you interact with any of the hotel staff — everyone I spoke to, from front desk staff to custodians, was beyond friendly.

As for amenities, they align with the brand’s laid-back, outdoorsy style and with some of the things the Mendocino area is known for. You’ll find:

Located just a few minutes’ walk (or bike ride) from downtown Mendocino, Hill House at Trailborn puts guests in the heart of the town’s charming boutiques and varied dining and drinking scene. But you won’t get bored if you hang around the property, either.

Here are some of the on-site activities guests may want to try:

While Mendocino’s remoteness makes it a haven for crowd-weary travelers, it’s becoming easier than ever to reach thanks to recent roadwork funding and new direct flights to Charles M. Schulz–Sonoma County Airport (STS), including on Alaska Airlines, Delta and Southwest. That’s one reason Mendo made TPG’s 2027 Where to Go list.

But travelers can also fly into San Francisco International Airport (SFO), Oakland San Francisco Bay Airport (OAK) or Sacramento International Airport (SAC), which are a bit farther away but offer more flight options.

Depending on the airport you choose, you’ll need to rent a car and drive two to four hours to Mendocino.

Basic rooms start as low as $140 per night in the off-season, while my King Junior Suite Ocean View starts around $350 per night (though these prices can climb much higher on summer weekends). Award rates start at 48,000 Marriott Bonvoy points per night, or you could redeem a 50,000-point free night certificate.

When booking, you’ll want to use one of the credit cards that earn the most points for Marriott stays, as well as one that possibly offers automatic Marriott Bonvoy elite status for value-added benefits. These include:

The information for the Marriott Bonvoy Bountiful card has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer.

Hill House has three wheelchair-accessible rooms, including two double queens and one king; these feature accessible tubs and, in some cases, roll-in showers. The property and its parking lot are also wheelchair accessible. For hearing-impaired guests, a portable kit can be installed in any room.

As a points traveler who loves Mendocino, I’m thrilled to see the town’s first points property not only opening but thriving. As a traveler who appreciates unique stays and has experienced some of the town’s charming independent properties, I’m also glad that Hill House at Trailborn Mendocino has brought enough character to fit seamlessly into the local scene.

It seems the Trailborn brand — and Marriott Bonvoy — is betting big on Mendocino. Hill House is one of two Mendocino properties purchased by The Trailborn brand. The second, the 150-year-old Mendocino Hotel, is undergoing renovation and slated to open in 2027.

#6159. This week: Permitting bill hits Senate floor amid aviation funding fight

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., last week formally launched a leadership challenge to Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo)

The lame-duck session continues as lawmakers look ahead to Thanksgiving and the funding deadline that arrives in December. The primary legislative business this week is the Senate's bipartisan permitting overhaul, but a late-breaking aviation funding fight and the Senate Democratic leadership contest are also commanding attention.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., last week formally launched a leadership challenge to Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y., and both men are accumulating supporters ahead of leadership votes that are currently scheduled for early December — though there's been an effort to move that up to this week.

Van Hollen has expressed disagreement with Schumer's participation in primaries.

​"I don't think it's the role of the Senate majority leader to get involved in open, contested Democratic primaries," Van Hollen said Sunday on CNN.

​Van Hollen has also said he wants to use all available tools to stop funding for the Iran war immediately, with a government funding deadline in December. That's going to be one of several flash points for December's funding discussions, as President Donald Trump and congressional Republicans try to use what leverage they have before Democrats take the gavels in the House and the Senate in January.

A new issue is the state of federal air traffic control after Friday's nationwide ground stop, with the Trump administration now seeking $50 billion to upgrade systems.

"I need additional money to do the additional work to keep the airspace safe," Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said on Fox News Sunday.

Sen. Brian Schatz, D-Hawaii, a senior appropriator who is in line to become majority whip, has suggested reallocating funds from the additional money the Trump administration and congressional Republicans allocated to Immigration and Customs Enforcement to address the challenges at the Federal Aviation Administration.

"There is a pot of 60 billion extra dollars on top of the regularly appropriated amount for ICE and we should use at least a portion of that money for the FAA. We can solve this problem and not spend any additional taxpayer dollars," Schatz posted on X.

"We can do all things, we don't have to do one versus the other," Duffy said in the Fox News Sunday interview. "I don't think that is the answer. The answer is let's do everything that's going to keep Americans safe, whether it's with immigration or it's with air travel."

Meanwhile on the Senate floor, the energy permitting overhaul bill faces a key test Monday evening​, with a vote scheduled to limit debate on a substitute amendment that represents the most recent version of the bill. Votes on a number of President Donald Trump's judicial nominations are also lined up this week.

On the other side of the Capitol, the House floor schedule i​ncludes several labor-related bills. ​One of the measures, introduced by Sen.-elect Kevin Hern, R-Okla.,​ would set standards for the way labor law applies to franchise operators.

New member orientation is also continuing, and committees in both the House and Senate will be holding hearings throughout the week as the outgoing Republican committee chairs aim to get through priority items on their agenda before the end of the Congress.

That includes a Tuesday morning Senate Armed Services Committee confirmation hearing for Hung Cao, the nominee to be Navy secretary, who is currently the acting secretary. The Senate Judiciary Committee will be busy as well, as Chairman Charles E. Grassley, R-Iowa, looks to tee up more of Trump's judicial nominations for floor consideration.
